article.title: Shoulder Arthritis Exercises: A Complete UK Physiotherapy Guide
article.excerpt: UK physiotherapist-approved exercises for shoulder arthritis. Step-by-step strengthening, range-of-motion and stretching exercises to reduce pain and improve mobility.
article.content:
Shoulder arthritis affects approximately one in three people over 60 in the UK to some degree, making it one of the most common causes of shoulder pain and restricted movement. Whether you have osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis or post-traumatic arthritis of the shoulder, targeted exercises can significantly reduce pain, improve range of motion and help you maintain independence for daily tasks like dressing, reaching and driving. This guide provides UK physiotherapist-approved exercises specifically designed for shoulder arthritis.

Quick answer: Shoulder arthritis exercises can significantly reduce pain and improve movement, benefiting conditions like osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or post-traumatic arthritis. Key exercises include pendulum swings, wall crawls, and behind-the-back reaches to improve range of motion. Gentle strengthening can be achieved with resistance band external rotations, shoulder blade squeezes, and wall press-ups. Always warm up, move gently, and stop if you experience sharp or worsening pain.

Understanding Shoulder Arthritis

The shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body, with an extraordinary range of motion that allows you to reach, lift, throw and rotate your arm in almost any direction. This mobility comes at a cost — the shoulder relies heavily on muscles, tendons and ligaments for stability rather than bony architecture, making it vulnerable to wear, injury and arthritis.

There are two joints in the shoulder complex that can be affected by arthritis: the glenohumeral joint (the main ball-and-socket joint where the upper arm meets the shoulder blade) and the acromioclavicular (AC) joint (where the collarbone meets the top of the shoulder blade). AC joint arthritis is particularly common and often causes pain when reaching across the body or overhead.

Symptoms of Shoulder Arthritis

  • Deep, aching pain in the shoulder joint, often worse at night
  • Stiffness, particularly in the morning or after periods of inactivity
  • Reduced range of motion — difficulty reaching behind your back, overhead or across your body
  • Grinding, clicking or crepitus during movement
  • Pain with activities like dressing, washing hair, reaching shelves or driving
  • Weakness in the affected arm

Before You Start: Important Guidelines

  • Warm up first — apply a warm flannel or heat pack to the shoulder for 10 minutes before exercising
  • Move gently — never force a painful movement. Work within your comfortable range
  • Consistency beats intensity — daily gentle exercise is better than occasional vigorous sessions
  • Pain monitoring — mild discomfort during exercise is acceptable, but sharp or worsening pain means stop
  • If pain persists more than 2 hours after exercising, you've done too much — reduce intensity next time
  • Consult your GP or physiotherapist before starting if you've had recent shoulder surgery or injection

Range-of-Motion Exercises

These exercises aim to maintain or improve the movement available in your shoulder joint. Perform each exercise 5–10 times, twice daily.

1. Pendulum Swings

Lean forward with your good hand on a table for support. Let the affected arm hang freely. Gently swing the arm in small circles — clockwise for 30 seconds, then anticlockwise for 30 seconds. Gradually increase the circle size as comfort allows. You can hold a small tin of beans (400g) to add gentle traction. This exercise uses gravity to decompress the joint and is excellent for warming up.

2. Wall Crawl (Forward)

Stand facing a wall at arm's length. Place the fingertips of your affected hand on the wall at waist height. Slowly "crawl" your fingers up the wall as high as comfortable. Hold at the top for 5 seconds, then crawl back down. Mark your progress with a small piece of tape — this gives you a visual target to work towards over weeks.

3. Wall Crawl (Side)

Stand sideways to the wall with your affected shoulder closest. Repeat the crawling motion out to the side. This targets a different plane of movement (abduction) that is often restricted in shoulder arthritis.

4. Behind-the-Back Reach

Hold a towel behind your back with both hands — the good arm reaches over the shoulder, the affected arm reaches up from below. Gently pull upward with the good arm to guide the affected arm into a stretch. Hold for 10–15 seconds. This mimics the movement needed for fastening a bra, tucking in a shirt or reaching a back pocket.

5. Cross-Body Stretch

Use your good arm to gently pull the affected arm across your body at chest height. You should feel a stretch at the back and side of the shoulder. Hold for 15–20 seconds. This targets the posterior capsule, which often tightens in shoulder arthritis.

Strengthening Exercises

Once range of motion improves, gentle strengthening helps support and protect the joint. Use light resistance bands (available from pharmacies and online, £5–£15) or small weights (0.5–1 kg to start).

1. Isometric External Rotation

Stand sideways to a wall with the affected arm closest. Bend your elbow to 90 degrees and place the back of your hand against the wall. Push gently into the wall (as if trying to rotate your arm outward) and hold for 10 seconds. This strengthens the rotator cuff without moving the painful joint. Repeat 10 times.

2. Resistance Band External Rotation

Anchor a resistance band at elbow height (a door handle works well). Hold the band with the affected arm, elbow bent to 90 degrees and tucked into your side. Rotate your forearm outward against the band's resistance, then slowly return. Keep the elbow glued to your side throughout. Perform 2 sets of 10 repetitions.

3. Shoulder Blade Squeezes

Sit or stand with good posture. Squeeze your shoulder blades together as if trying to hold a pencil between them. Hold for 5 seconds, then relax. This strengthens the muscles that stabilise the shoulder blade, providing a better foundation for shoulder movement. Repeat 15 times.

4. Wall Press-Up

Stand an arm's length from a wall, hands at shoulder height. Slowly bend your elbows to lean towards the wall, then push back. This gently strengthens the chest and front shoulder muscles. Perform 2 sets of 10 repetitions. Progress by standing further from the wall.

Daily Activities and Adaptations

  • Dressing — Put the affected arm into sleeves first; use front-fastening clothes; try a dressing stick or long-handled shoe horn
  • Reaching — Use a grabber/reacher for high shelves; reorganise cupboards to keep frequently used items at waist to shoulder height
  • Sleeping — Try sleeping on your back with a pillow under the affected arm, or on the unaffected side with a pillow hugging the affected arm
  • Driving — Adjust your seat and mirrors to minimise reaching; consider a steering wheel cover for easier grip

When to Seek Further Help

See your GP if shoulder pain is severe or worsening despite exercises, you have sudden inability to lift your arm (possible rotator cuff tear), you experience numbness or tingling down the arm, or shoulder pain is disrupting sleep consistently. Your GP can refer you to NHS physiotherapy (typically 4–8 weeks wait) or an orthopaedic specialist if needed. Treatments may include corticosteroid injections, hyaluronic acid injections or, in severe cases, shoulder replacement surgery.

Consistent, gentle exercise is the single most effective long-term treatment for shoulder arthritis. Start slowly, be patient with progress and celebrate small improvements. Our virtual assistant can help you create a personalised shoulder exercise programme.

This article is for general information only. Consult a physiotherapist or GP before starting exercises if you have severe shoulder pain or have had recent surgery.

Shoulder Exercises for Osteoarthritis

For shoulder (glenohumeral) osteoarthritis, the priority is restoring pain-free range of motion before adding load. Pendulum swings, wall slides and supine external rotation with a light band are the safest starting points. See our osteoarthritis exercises guide and osteoarthritis treatment overview.

Shoulder Exercises for Rheumatoid Arthritis

Shoulder RA responds best to a low-load, high-repetition approach. During flares, restrict to pendulums and supported range of motion only. Resume strengthening when the joint is no longer warm. See rheumatoid arthritis exercises.

Gentle Shoulder Exercises for Severe Arthritis

Pendulum swings, supported table slides, gentle scapular squeezes and warm-water exercise allow you to keep the shoulder moving without overloading the joint. Two short 10-minute daily sessions are usually better tolerated than one longer one.

Shoulder Exercises After Replacement

After shoulder replacement (anatomic or reverse), follow your surgeon's protocol precisely for the first 6–12 weeks. The strengthening routine on this page typically becomes appropriate beyond 12 weeks, once cleared by your surgical team.

Exercises to Avoid With Shoulder Arthritis

Avoid behind-the-neck lat pulldowns, military presses, upright rows, heavy bench press and any overhead lifting with poor technique. Replace with band external rotation, wall push-ups and seated rows. For a personalised plan, find a shoulder physiotherapist near you.

Shoulder Arthritis Exercise FAQ — People Also Ask

What are the best exercises for arthritic shoulders?

The best routine combines pendulum swings and wall slides (mobility), band external rotation and scapular squeezes (strength), and warm-up with a heat pack for 10 minutes. Done 3–4 times per week, this combination reduces pain and improves overhead reach.

How often should I do shoulder exercises for arthritis?

Mobility daily (5–10 minutes), strengthening 2–3 times per week. Allow at least one rest day between strengthening sessions.

Can exercise cure shoulder arthritis?

No — exercise cannot reverse cartilage loss, but it is the most effective non-surgical treatment and can delay the need for shoulder replacement. Benefits stop if exercise stops.

What shoulder exercises should I avoid with arthritis?

Avoid behind-the-neck lat pulldowns, military presses, upright rows and heavy overhead lifting. Replace with band external rotation, wall push-ups and seated rows.

Are there gentle shoulder exercises for severe arthritis?

Yes — pendulum swings, supported table slides, scapular squeezes and warm-water exercise. Two short 10-minute daily sessions are usually better tolerated.

How long until shoulder exercises reduce arthritis pain?

Reduced stiffness within 2–3 weeks, meaningful pain reduction at 6–8 weeks, full benefit at 12 weeks of consistent practice.

article.title: Best Walking Shoes for Arthritis in the UK
article.excerpt: Find the best walking shoes for arthritis in the UK. Expert guide to cushioning, arch support, and easy-fasten features for painful feet and joints.
article.content:
Choosing the right walking shoes can make a significant difference when living with arthritis. The wrong footwear can increase joint stress, while well-designed shoes provide cushioning, support, and stability that reduce pain during daily activities.

Quick answer: For arthritis, choose walking shoes with a cushioned midsole for impact absorption and good arch support for alignment. A wide toe box allows natural toe spread, and lightweight materials reduce effort. Look for non-slip soles for balance and easy fastenings like Velcro for stiff hands. A removable insole is useful for custom orthotics.

What to Look for in Arthritis-Friendly Shoes

  • Cushioned midsole — absorbs impact and reduces stress on knees, hips, and feet
  • Good arch support — maintains proper foot alignment and reduces fatigue
  • Wide toe box — allows toes to spread naturally, especially important for bunions or toe deformities
  • Lightweight — reduces the effort needed to lift each foot
  • Non-slip sole — important for balance and fall prevention
  • Easy fastening — Velcro straps, zip closures, or slip-on designs for stiff hands
  • Removable insole — allows you to use custom orthotics if prescribed

Features by Arthritis Type

For Foot & Ankle Arthritis

Prioritise extra cushioning, a rocker sole (gently curved bottom), and a structured heel counter for ankle stability.

For Knee & Hip Arthritis

Focus on shock absorption and avoid completely flat shoes. A slight heel-to-toe drop (8-12mm) can help with natural walking motion.

For Hand Arthritis

Choose shoes with Velcro closures, pull-on loops, or elastic laces to avoid the need for tying.

Where to Buy in the UK

  • Hotter Shoes — UK brand specialising in comfort footwear with wide fittings
  • Cosyfeet — extra-roomy shoes designed for problem feet
  • Skechers — memory foam insoles and slip-on styles widely available
  • New Balance — excellent range of wide-fitting walking shoes
  • Clarks — UK high street staple with supportive designs

NHS Footwear Services

If arthritis significantly affects your feet, your GP can refer you to an NHS podiatrist or orthotist. They can provide:

  • Custom orthotics (insoles) shaped to your feet
  • Specialist medical-grade footwear
  • Advice on shoe modifications

This article is for general information. Consult a podiatrist or physiotherapist for personalised footwear advice.

article.title: How to Get Arthritis Physiotherapy on the NHS Waiting List
article.excerpt: A practical guide to getting arthritis physiotherapy on the NHS — including self-referral, what to expect and how to manage while you wait.
article.content:
Getting arthritis physiotherapy on the NHS waiting list is simpler than many people realise. In many areas, you can self-refer without a GP appointment — and while you wait, there are evidence-based steps you can take immediately.

Quick answer: Many NHS areas offer direct physiotherapy self-referral for arthritis — no GP needed. Search "physiotherapy self-referral" plus your area on NHS.uk. Waiting times are typically 4-16 weeks for routine cases.

Physiotherapy assessment — openly licensed via Openverse

NHS Physiotherapy Self-Referral

Many NHS Integrated Care Boards (ICBs) now offer direct access to physiotherapy without requiring a GP referral first. This is called self-referral or direct access. To check whether it is available in your area: search "physiotherapy self-referral" plus your county or town on NHS.uk, or call your local GP surgery and ask whether they use a self-referral physiotherapy service.

Self-referral typically means calling or completing an online form directly with the physiotherapy department. You will be triaged — usually by phone — to determine urgency and appropriate pathway.

If You Need a GP Referral

If self-referral is not available locally, ask your GP to refer you to the NHS MSK (musculoskeletal) physiotherapy service. Be specific: describe how your arthritis affects daily activities, work and sleep. Functional impact language (rather than pain scores alone) tends to result in faster triage.

Physiotherapy session — openly licensed via Openverse

Typical Waiting Times

NHS physiotherapy waiting times vary significantly by area. As of 2026, routine waits range from 4 to 16 weeks. Urgent cases (e.g. severe functional limitation, post-surgical rehabilitation) are typically seen within 2–4 weeks.

What to Do While You Wait

  • Use Versus Arthritis free exercise guides (versusarthritis.org) for condition-specific home exercise sheets.
  • Access the Living With Arthritis UK exercise hub (livingwitharthritis.org.uk/exercises) for guided programmes.
  • Consider a single private physiotherapy assessment (£50–80) to get a programme started immediately.

Home exercise while waiting — openly licensed via Openverse

Q&A

Question: Can I get physiotherapy for any arthritis type?
Short answer: Yes. NHS physiotherapy is available for all arthritis types including OA, RA, PsA and AS. The programme will be tailored to your specific condition and joint involvement.

Question: How many sessions will I get?
Short answer: Typically 4–6 sessions on the NHS, though this varies. The aim is to give you a home programme you can continue independently.

article.title: Signs of Rheumatoid Arthritis in Early Stages
article.excerpt: Recognising the early signs of rheumatoid arthritis is critical — early treatment significantly reduces long-term joint damage. Here is what to look for.
article.content:
Signs of rheumatoid arthritis in early stages are often subtle and easily dismissed as general aches or tiredness. Recognising them early is one of the most important things you can do — early DMARD treatment significantly reduces joint damage and improves long-term outcomes.

Quick answer: Early signs of RA include: symmetrical swelling in small hand/foot joints, morning stiffness lasting over 30-60 minutes, profound fatigue and flu-like malaise. See your GP urgently if symptoms persist over 6 weeks — NICE recommends rheumatology referral within 3 working days.

Rheumatoid arthritis — openly licensed via Openverse

The Classic Early Warning Signs

Symmetrical Joint Swelling

RA typically begins in the small joints of the hands and feet — the knuckle joints (MCPs), middle finger joints (PIPs) and the joints at the balls of the feet (MTPs). The key distinguishing feature is symmetry: both wrists, both sets of knuckles. If your right hand is affected, your left usually is too.

Prolonged Morning Stiffness

Morning stiffness lasting more than 30–60 minutes — often described as hands feeling "locked" or "wrapped in bandages" — is a cardinal early sign of RA. This distinguishes it from osteoarthritis, where stiffness typically resolves within 30 minutes.

Fatigue and Flu-Like Malaise

Many people with early RA report profound fatigue before joint symptoms become prominent. Low-grade fever, loss of appetite and general unwellness are caused by the same inflammatory cytokines attacking the joint lining.

Arthritic hand changes — openly licensed via Openverse

Blood Tests Used in Early RA

Your GP will typically test for: CRP and ESR (inflammatory markers), rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-CCP antibodies. Crucially, up to 30% of early RA is seronegative — blood tests may be normal. A negative test does not rule out RA if clinical features are present.

What to Do If You Recognise These Signs

If you have had persistent swelling or stiffness in small hand or foot joints for more than six weeks, see your GP as soon as possible. NICE guidance recommends urgent referral to rheumatology within three working days for suspected inflammatory arthritis.

Early assessment — openly licensed via Openverse

Q&A

Question: How quickly does RA progress if untreated?
Short answer: Joint erosion can begin within weeks to months of symptom onset in untreated RA. This is why early DMARD treatment is so important.

Question: Can RA start at any age?
Short answer: Yes — RA can start at any age including childhood. Peak adult onset is between 40 and 60 years.

article.title: Arthritis in Young People – UK Guide
article.excerpt: Arthritis doesn't just affect older adults. Learn about juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) and other types affecting young people in the UK, plus where to find support.
article.content:
Arthritis is often thought of as a condition affecting older adults, but in the UK, around 15,000 children and young people are living with arthritis. Understanding the condition and accessing the right support is crucial for managing symptoms and maintaining quality of life.

Quick answer: Arthritis can affect young people, with around 15,000 children and young people in the UK living with the condition. Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) is the most common form in under-16s, causing joint pain, swelling, and stiffness. Symptoms can include morning stiffness, fatigue, and fevers. Early diagnosis by a GP and paediatric rheumatologist is important for managing the condition.

Types of Arthritis in Young People

Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA)

JIA is the most common type of arthritis in under-16s. "Idiopathic" means the cause is unknown. There are several subtypes:

  • Oligoarticular JIA — affects 4 or fewer joints, most common type
  • Polyarticular JIA — affects 5 or more joints
  • Systemic JIA — causes whole-body symptoms including fevers and rash
  • Enthesitis-related JIA — affects where tendons attach to bone
  • Psoriatic JIA — associated with the skin condition psoriasis

Reactive Arthritis

Can develop after an infection and usually resolves within weeks to months.

Young Adult Onset

Rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and other inflammatory types can begin in the late teens or twenties.

Recognising Symptoms

  • Joint pain, swelling, or stiffness lasting more than 6 weeks
  • Limping or reluctance to use a limb (in younger children)
  • Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes
  • Fatigue beyond normal tiredness
  • Unexplained fevers with joint symptoms

Getting Diagnosed in the UK

If you suspect arthritis in a child or young person:

  1. See your GP — describe all symptoms and how long they've lasted
  2. Request a referral to a paediatric rheumatologist
  3. NHS waiting times vary — ask about urgent referral if symptoms are severe

UK Support Resources

  • JIGSAW (Joint Involvement Group for Self-Advocacy Workshops)
  • NRAS (National Rheumatoid Arthritis Society) — resources for young people
  • Young people's rheumatology clinics — many NHS trusts run dedicated youth clinics
  • School support — children with JIA may qualify for an EHCP (Education, Health and Care Plan)

Living Well as a Young Person with Arthritis

  • Stay as active as possible — swimming and cycling are excellent
  • Talk to teachers and employers about reasonable adjustments
  • Connect with peers online — social support reduces isolation
  • Transition planning — move from paediatric to adult rheumatology services smoothly

If you're a young person with persistent joint symptoms, don't delay seeking help. Early treatment can prevent joint damage and improve long-term outcomes.

article.title: Best Plantar Fasciitis Shoes for Women (UK Guide, 2026)
article.excerpt: A UK-focused guide to choosing supportive shoes for plantar fasciitis: the eight features that matter, indicative £ prices, insoles, daily stretches and when to see a GP or physio.
article.content:
Quick answer: Plantar fasciitis is inflammation of the tissue band along the foot's sole, affecting around 1 in 10 adults. Supportive footwear, combined with stretches, often reduces pain within 4–8 weeks. Key shoe features include firm arch support, medium-firm cushioning, a deep heel cup, rigid heel counter, and an 8–12mm heel-to-toe drop, which can improve symptoms within weeks.

# Best Plantar Fasciitis Shoes for Women — A UK Guide for 2026 That sharp, stabbing pain in your heel during the first steps out of bed is one of the most recognisable signs of **plantar fasciitis** — an inflammation of the thick band of tissue that runs along the sole of your foot. It affects roughly **1 in 10 adults** at some point in life, and women between the ages of 40 and 60 are most commonly affected. The good news: for the majority of people, the right everyday footwear, combined with simple stretches, reduces pain significantly within **4–8 weeks** — no prescription required. This guide explains what to look for, which features actually matter, and how to combine supportive shoes with the rest of the conservative care plan that GPs and physiotherapists recommend in the UK. > **General guidance only.** This article is educational and is not a substitute for a clinical assessment. If your heel pain is severe, lasts longer than a few weeks, or you have diabetes, an inflammatory arthritis or any wound on the foot, please speak to your GP, a registered podiatrist or a HCPC-registered physiotherapist before changing footwear or starting exercises. ## Why footwear matters so much The plantar fascia is loaded every time you take a step. Shoes that fail to support the arch or absorb impact force the fascia to do that work on its own, which keeps the tissue inflamed and slows healing. Supportive shoes help in four ways: - **Arch support** spreads pressure evenly across the foot, reducing strain on the fascia. - **Cushioning** absorbs impact so the inflamed tissue is not repeatedly stressed. - **A deep, firm heel cup** keeps the heel stable and aligned with the leg. - **Pronation control** limits the inward roll of the foot that lengthens the fascia further. Most people who switch from unsupportive footwear (flat plimsolls, worn trainers, flip-flops, ballet pumps) to a properly supportive shoe notice a meaningful reduction in morning pain within two to three weeks. ## Eight features to look for When you pick up a shoe in the shop or order one online, work through this checklist: 1. **Firm arch support.** Press the inside of the arch with your thumb — it should resist the pressure rather than collapse. 2. **Medium-firm cushioning** through the heel and forefoot. Too soft is as unhelpful as too hard. 3. **A deep heel cup** that cradles the heel and stops it sliding. 4. **A rigid heel counter** — squeeze the back of the shoe; it should not crush easily. 5. **A stable midfoot.** Twist the shoe along its long axis. It should flex at the ball of the foot, not in the middle. 6. **A heel-to-toe drop of roughly 8–12 mm.** A small heel lift reduces pull on the fascia. 7. **A breathable upper** (mesh or soft leather) to keep feet dry through the day. 8. **A reasonable weight** so you can wear them all day without fatigue. If a shoe ticks at least six of these eight boxes, it is a sensible starting point. ## Categories of shoe to consider The same biomechanical principles apply across categories, so the right "best shoe" depends on what you'll mostly be doing in it. Below are well-regarded examples; they are illustrations of features, not endorsements, and other brands offer similar specifications. ### Everyday trainers and walking shoes (~£110–£170) Cushioned stability trainers with a guidance system through the midsole are the most widely recommended option. Models in this class — for example the ASICS Gel-Kayano, Brooks Adrenaline GTS or New Balance 990 — pair gel or EVA cushioning with a firmer medial post that gently corrects overpronation. They suit office wear with smart-casual outfits, school runs, long days on your feet, and gentle gym work. ### Clinically designed comfort shoes (~£100–£140) Brands such as Vionic and Orthofeet build orthotic-style arch support into the shoe itself, which means you often do not need to add an insole. They are a good fit if you want maximum support straight out of the box and don't run. ### Maximum-cushion shoes (~£140–£180) Maximalist designs such as Hoka's Bondi or Clifton have a very thick midsole and a "rocker" sole that rolls the foot forward as you walk. They suit people who feel they need more shock absorption — heavier users, those who spend hours on hard floors, or anyone with combined knee, hip and heel pain. ### Running shoes (~£120–£170) If you run, choose a **stability** running shoe (not a minimalist or "barefoot" model). Look for the same arch support, deep heel cup and 8–12 mm drop, plus durable rubber under the heel. ### Sandals, slippers and indoor shoes Morning pain often starts the moment you put on a flat slipper. Replace soft slippers and flip-flops with **contoured, arch-supportive** versions (Vionic, FitFlop, Orthofeet, Spenco are common examples). Wear them from the moment you get out of bed — not after you've already walked barefoot across the bedroom. ## Insoles and orthotics Quality insoles can extend a shoe's life and add support where you need it. They are particularly useful for work shoes that lack built-in support. - **Firm orthotic insoles** (Superfeet Green, Powerstep Pinnacle): the strongest off-the-shelf support, around £30–£50. - **Thinner orthotic insoles** (SOLE Active Thin, Pedag Viva): fit inside smart shoes and lower-volume trainers. - **Custom orthotics** from a registered podiatrist: usually £150–£400, recommended only if off-the-shelf insoles have not helped after six to eight weeks of consistent use. Choose insoles to match the **shoe's depth** and your **arch height**. A high-arched foot needs a contoured insole rather than a flat cushioned one. ## A simple weekly plan Footwear is most effective when paired with the basics that NICE-aligned UK physiotherapists recommend for plantar fasciitis: **Daily (10–15 minutes)** - Calf stretch against a wall — 3 × 30 seconds each leg. - Plantar-fascia stretch — pull the toes back gently for 30 seconds, repeat 3 times. - Towel or band stretch around the forefoot — 3 × 30 seconds. - Rolling the sole over a chilled water bottle for 5–10 minutes. **A few times a week** - Calf and intrinsic foot-muscle strengthening (heel raises, towel-scrunches). - Low-impact cardio: walking in supportive shoes, swimming, cycling, water-based exercise. **Habits to keep** - Avoid walking barefoot on hard floors. - Rotate between two pairs of supportive shoes so the cushioning can recover. - Replace running and walking shoes every roughly 500–800 km, or every 9–12 months of regular use. ## When to see a clinician Speak to a GP, registered podiatrist or HCPC-registered physiotherapist if: - Pain persists or worsens after 6–8 weeks of supportive shoes and daily stretching. - The pain is severe enough to wake you at night or you cannot bear weight on the heel. - You notice swelling, heat or redness, or have a wound on the foot. - You have diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, gout or another inflammatory condition. - The pain follows a fall or sudden injury — to rule out a heel-bone or fascia tear. Options at that point may include a guided stretching programme, a referral for custom orthotics, a night splint, ultrasound-guided injections or — very rarely — surgical release. ## Frequently asked questions **How long until I notice a difference?** Most people experience meaningful reduction in morning pain within 2–3 weeks of consistent wear. Full resolution typically takes 6–12 weeks alongside stretching. **Can I keep wearing my old trainers?** If they are worn in the heel, no longer offer firm arch support, or have a soft, collapsed midsole, they are likely to keep the inflammation going. Replace them. **Are expensive shoes always better?** No. The features above matter more than price. A well-chosen £110 shoe will outperform a £200 fashion trainer for plantar-fascia pain. **Are custom orthotics worth it?** For most people, off-the-shelf insoles plus a good shoe are enough. If you've tried both consistently for six to eight weeks without improvement, a podiatrist-prescribed orthotic is a reasonable next step. **Should I rotate between two pairs of shoes?** Yes. Cushioning recovers more fully with 24 hours' rest, so rotating two pairs extends their useful life and gives more consistent support. **Can children get plantar fasciitis?** True plantar fasciitis is uncommon in children. Heel pain in active children is more often Sever's disease (irritation at the growth plate). Speak to a GP if heel pain persists. **Will it come back?** Plantar fasciitis can recur if you return to unsupportive footwear or stop the stretching routine. Keep one supportive pair as your everyday default and continue calf and foot stretches several times a week, even after the pain has gone. ## Take-home checklist - ✅ Choose a shoe with firm arch support, a deep heel cup and a rigid midfoot. - ✅ Wear supportive shoes from the moment you get up — not after walking barefoot. - ✅ Pair shoes with daily calf and plantar-fascia stretches. - ✅ Replace tired trainers and avoid flat unsupportive footwear. - ✅ See a GP, podiatrist or physiotherapist if there's no improvement in 6–8 weeks. Your feet carry you through every part of life with arthritis — and through the rest of life as well. A well-chosen pair of shoes is one of the simplest, most evidence-friendly steps you can take to look after them.

article.content:
Quick answer: Shoulder arthroscopy will not cure arthritis or reverse joint damage. Evidence shows short-term benefits for some impingement, but it is not significantly better than non-surgical approaches long-term. For moderate to severe arthritis, arthroscopy offers little lasting benefit. It is typically reserved for specific situations when conservative methods like physical therapy, medication, and injections have failed.

## Overview Useful for some impingement; less so for advanced arthritis. ## What the evidence shows UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Versus Arthritis consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus. ## What this means for you - **Talk to your clinician.** Personalised advice always beats blanket rules. - **Track your symptoms.** Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days. - **Move within comfort.** Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood. - **Watch the warning signs.** New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review. ## Practical next steps 1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: [related guidance](/exercises/shoulder). 2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment. 3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day. ## Editorial standards This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis Editorial Team and reviewed by our Clinical Review Board against UK NICE guidance and peer-reviewed sources. We update content at least annually. ## What the Evidence Says Systematic reviews looking at shoulder arthroscopy for common arthritis-related shoulder problems, such as impingement, generally show mixed results. While some people report short-term pain relief and improved function, these benefits often aren't significantly better than non-surgical approaches like physical therapy and targeted exercises in the long run. For moderate to severe arthritis where there's significant joint damage, randomised trials consistently demonstrate that arthroscopy offers little to no lasting benefit compared to managing symptoms with medication, injections, and rehabilitation. Clinical guidelines from professional bodies across the UK increasingly advocate for conservative management as the first line of treatment. Surgery is typically reserved for very specific situations where non-surgical methods have failed over an extended period, and where the type of arthritis and extent of joint damage suggest a reasonable chance of success. This evidence-based approach aims to prevent unnecessary procedures and the associated risks. ## Common Mistakes to Avoid * **Delaying physical therapy:** Waiting too long to start guided exercises can make stiffness worse. Start gentle, consistent movement as soon as discomfort allows. * **Overdoing it too soon after a flare-up:** Pushing through significant pain can inflame the joint further. Listen to your body and respect pain as a warning signal. * **Relying solely on painkillers:** Medication can help manage pain but doesn't address the underlying joint health or restore function. Combine with movement and other therapies. * **Ignoring changes in symptoms:** Dismissing new or worsening pain, grinding, or clicking as 'just arthritis' can miss treatable issues. Keep your healthcare professional informed of any significant changes. * **Not discussing expectations with your surgeon:** Assuming surgery will 'fix everything' can lead to disappointment. Understand the realistic outcomes and limitations of any procedure. ## When to Speak to a Clinician It's important to keep your GP, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist updated about your shoulder pain and symptoms. While some discomfort is part of living with arthritis, certain signs warrant a prompt discussion to make sure nothing serious is developing. Don't hesitate to reach out if you experience any of the following: * Sudden, severe pain that wasn't there before. * Inability to move your arm or shoulder at all. * Redness, warmth, or swelling around the joint, especially with a fever. * Pain that wakes you from sleep or is constant, even at rest. * Numbness, tingling, or weakness spreading down your arm. ## Frequently Asked Questions ### Will shoulder arthroscopy cure my arthritis? No, shoulder arthroscopy typically will not cure arthritis. For certain types of arthritis, it might help manage specific symptoms like impingement or remove loose fragments of cartilage, but it doesn't reverse joint damage or prevent further progression of the disease. ### How long does recovery from shoulder arthroscopy take? Recovery times vary highly depending on the extent of the procedure and individual healing. Generally, it can take several weeks to a few months of guided physical therapy to regain strength and movement, with full recovery sometimes taking up to six months or longer. ### What are the alternatives to shoulder arthroscopy for arthritis? Alternatives include a comprehensive physical therapy programme, pain relief medication, steroid injections into the joint, lifestyle adjustments, and, in some severe cases, open surgery such as a shoulder replacement for extensive joint damage. ### Practical next steps for Shoulder Arthroscopy and Arthritis: What It Can and Can't Fix If you came here about **Shoulder Arthroscopy and Arthritis: What It Can and Can't Fix**, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live. ### Preparing for appointments Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book. ### Preparing for appointments Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. article.title: Spinal Arthritis and Back Pain UK: Symptoms, Treatment and Self-Help
article.excerpt: UK guide to spinal arthritis and back pain. Understand spondylosis symptoms, NHS diagnosis, exercises for spinal OA and when to see your GP about back stiffness.
article.content:
Spinal arthritis — medically known as spondylosis — is one of the most common causes of chronic back and neck pain in the UK. Affecting the facet joints, discs and vertebrae of the spine, it's estimated that over 80% of people over 40 show some evidence of spinal degeneration on X-ray, though not all experience symptoms. This guide explains what spinal arthritis is, how it's diagnosed, and provides practical self-help strategies recommended by UK healthcare professionals.

Quick answer: Spinal arthritis, also known as spondylosis, affects the facet joints, discs, and vertebrae of the spine, causing chronic back and neck pain. Symptoms include stiffness, reduced flexibility, and pain that improves with gentle movement. Management involves exercises such as pelvic tilts and chin tucks, maintaining good posture, and sometimes physiotherapy or pain medication. Seek urgent medical attention for loss of bladder/bowel control or sudden weakness.

What Is Spinal Arthritis?

The spine is made up of 33 vertebrae connected by facet joints at the back and intervertebral discs at the front. Spinal arthritis most commonly involves osteoarthritis of the facet joints (facet joint arthropathy) and degeneration of the intervertebral discs (degenerative disc disease). These changes occur naturally with age but can be accelerated by injury, genetics, obesity and occupational factors.

Areas Affected

  • Cervical spine (neck) — Causes neck pain, stiffness and sometimes headaches. May cause nerve compression leading to arm pain, tingling or weakness
  • Thoracic spine (mid-back) — Less commonly affected due to the stabilising effect of the rib cage
  • Lumbar spine (lower back) — The most common area for spinal arthritis, causing lower back pain, stiffness and sometimes leg symptoms (sciatica)

Symptoms

  • Stiffness and pain in the back or neck, worse in the morning and after inactivity
  • Pain that improves with gentle movement but worsens with prolonged standing or walking
  • Reduced flexibility — difficulty bending, twisting or looking over your shoulder
  • Grinding or crunching sensation (crepitus) with movement
  • Pain that radiates into the buttocks, hips or legs (lumbar) or shoulders and arms (cervical)
  • Numbness, tingling or weakness in limbs (if nerves are compressed — seek medical attention)

Exercises for Spinal Arthritis

Exercise is the cornerstone of spinal arthritis management. These exercises should be performed daily:

Lower Back

  • Pelvic tilts — Lie on your back with knees bent. Gently flatten your lower back against the floor by tightening your abdominal muscles. Hold 5 seconds, release. Repeat 15 times
  • Knee rolls — Lie on your back with knees bent. Slowly roll both knees to one side, keeping shoulders flat. Hold 10 seconds, then roll to the other side. Repeat 10 times each side
  • Cat-cow stretch — On hands and knees, slowly arch your back upward (cat), then dip it downward (cow). Move gently between positions 10 times
  • Bridge — Lie on your back, knees bent. Lift your hips off the floor until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees. Hold 5 seconds. Repeat 10 times

Neck

  • Chin tucks — Sit with good posture. Draw your chin straight back (creating a "double chin"). Hold 5 seconds. This strengthens deep neck flexors. Repeat 10 times
  • Gentle neck rotations — Slowly turn your head to look over each shoulder. Hold 5 seconds each side. Repeat 5 times
  • Neck side bends — Tilt your ear towards your shoulder (don't raise the shoulder). Hold 10 seconds each side

Core Strengthening

A strong core supports the spine and reduces load on arthritic joints:

  • Dead bug — Lie on your back, arms pointing to the ceiling, knees bent at 90°. Slowly extend one arm overhead while extending the opposite leg. Return and switch sides. 2 sets of 10
  • Side plank (modified) — Lie on your side, propped on your elbow, knees bent. Lift your hips off the floor. Hold 10–20 seconds. This targets the obliques that stabilise the spine

Posture and Ergonomics

  • Sit with your back supported — use a lumbar roll or rolled towel in the curve of your lower back
  • Adjust your computer screen to eye level to avoid sustained neck flexion
  • Take movement breaks every 30 minutes — prolonged sitting increases spinal stiffness
  • Sleep on a supportive mattress — medium-firm is generally recommended. Place a pillow between your knees when side-sleeping
  • Lift objects by bending your knees and keeping the load close to your body

NHS Treatment Options

  • Physiotherapy — Tailored exercise programmes, manual therapy and education. Available through GP referral
  • Pain medication — Paracetamol, NSAIDs (topical and oral), and sometimes neuropathic pain medications for nerve-related symptoms
  • Facet joint injections — Corticosteroid injections into the affected facet joints, performed by pain specialists or radiologists
  • Pain management programmes — Multidisciplinary programmes combining exercise, psychology and education
  • Surgery — Rarely needed. Options include decompression (removing bone pressing on nerves) or spinal fusion in severe cases

When to See Your GP Urgently

Most back pain from spinal arthritis is manageable, but see your GP urgently or attend A&E if you experience loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness in the genital/saddle area, sudden severe weakness in both legs, or worsening numbness/weakness in arms or legs. These symptoms may indicate cauda equina syndrome or cord compression, which require emergency assessment.

Spinal arthritis is extremely common and usually very manageable with regular exercise, good posture habits and appropriate treatment. Our virtual assistant can help you create a tailored back exercise programme.

This article is for general information only. See your GP for persistent back or neck pain, particularly if accompanied by leg or arm symptoms.

Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete. In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live. ### Working with NHS pathways Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates. ### Working with NHS pathways Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates. ### Using evidence carefully Marketing claims for joint supplements often outrun the research. Look for products that state dose clearly, avoid miracle language, and fit alongside — never instead of — prescribed treatment. Stop and seek advice if you notice bruising, stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or new rashes. ### Quick questions about Spinal Arthritis Back Pain **Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician?** No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team. **How long before I judge whether a change helped?** Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner. **What should I track?** Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. article.title: Staying Active with Arthritis in Winter: UK Guide to Cold-Weather Exercise
article.excerpt: How to stay active with arthritis during UK winters. Indoor exercise ideas, layering tips, warm-up routines and motivation strategies for cold weather joint pain.
article.content:
Winter in the UK presents a particular challenge for the millions of people living with arthritis. Shorter days, cold temperatures, icy conditions and the natural inclination to hibernate on the sofa can cause physical activity levels to plummet — yet staying active during winter is arguably more important than at any other time of year. Regular movement keeps joints lubricated, muscles strong, weight in check and mood elevated. This guide provides practical strategies for maintaining an active lifestyle throughout the British winter.

Quick answer: In winter, all adults in the UK should take a daily 10-microgram (400 IU) vitamin D supplement, as recommended by Public Health England. This is because between October and March, the UK does not receive enough sunlight for the body to produce sufficient vitamin D, which is vital for bone health, immune function, and may help reduce arthritis inflammation.

Why Winter Activity Matters More

The temptation to rest during cold weather is understandable, but inactivity creates a vicious cycle: less movement leads to stiffer joints, weaker muscles, weight gain and lower mood — all of which worsen arthritis symptoms. Research shows that physical activity levels in the UK drop by 20–30% during winter months, and this decline is even more pronounced among people with chronic pain conditions.

Conversely, maintaining activity through winter helps keep synovial fluid flowing (the joint's natural lubricant), prevent deconditioning and muscle loss, support mental health (combating seasonal affective disorder), maintain a healthy weight through the calorie-dense festive season, and reduce the severity and duration of morning stiffness.

Indoor Exercise Options

When outdoor conditions are poor, having indoor alternatives is essential.

Swimming and Aquatic Exercise

Indoor heated pools offer one of the best exercise environments for arthritis in winter. Warm water (typically 28–32°C) soothes joints, provides buoyancy that reduces weight-bearing stress by up to 90%, and allows movement that would be painful on land. Most UK leisure centres have heated indoor pools. Look for "aquafit" or "gentle aqua" classes specifically suited to people with joint conditions.

Home-Based Exercises

  • Chair-based exercises — Full-body workout from the comfort of your living room. NHS and Versus Arthritis have free YouTube videos
  • Yoga and tai chi — Online classes allow you to practice in a warm home environment
  • Resistance band exercises — Compact, affordable equipment for strength training at home
  • Stationary cycling — Pedal exercisers (from £20) sit on the floor and can be used from a chair
  • Stair exercises — If you have stairs, gentle step-ups using the bottom step provide excellent leg strengthening

Indoor Walking

  • Shopping centres — many open early for "mall walking" groups
  • Indoor athletics tracks (some leisure centres have these)
  • Walking on the spot or marching in place while watching television
  • Indoor walking videos on YouTube (Leslie Sansone's "Walk at Home" series is popular)

Exercising Outdoors Safely

If you prefer outdoor exercise, preparation is key:

Layering for Arthritis

  • Base layer — Moisture-wicking thermal underwear keeps skin dry
  • Middle layer — Fleece or wool for insulation
  • Outer layer — Windproof and waterproof jacket
  • Extremities — Thermal gloves (or arthritis compression gloves under warm gloves), warm hat, thermal socks. Heat loss through the head and hands significantly affects comfort
  • Hand warmers — Reusable gel hand warmers (£2–£5) or disposable warmers can be placed in gloves or pockets

Safety on Ice and Wet Surfaces

  • Wear shoes with good grip — look for deep treads and slip-resistant soles
  • Use walking poles for stability on icy paths
  • Walk on gritted surfaces where possible
  • Take smaller steps to maintain balance
  • Avoid walking after dark when ice is hard to see
  • Slip-on ice grippers for shoes (£5–£15 from outdoor shops) provide extra traction

Warming Up in Cold Weather

Cold muscles and joints need a longer warm-up in winter. Spend 10–15 minutes warming up indoors before heading out: march on the spot, do gentle arm circles, knee lifts and ankle rolls. This increases blood flow to muscles and synovial fluid production before exposing joints to cold temperatures.

Motivation Strategies

  • Schedule exercise — Treat it as an appointment you can't cancel
  • Exercise buddy — Accountability makes you more likely to show up, especially on cold, dark days
  • Midday exercise — Take advantage of daylight during lunch breaks. Even 15 minutes of walking at lunchtime helps
  • Track your activity — Use a simple diary or step counter. Seeing progress is motivating
  • Set winter-specific goals — Rather than comparing to summer activity levels, set realistic winter targets
  • Reward yourself — Plan something enjoyable after exercise: a warm bath, hot chocolate, favourite TV programme
  • Remember the benefits — Exercise improves mood within minutes, and the effects last hours. On the coldest, darkest days, you'll feel the benefit most

Vitamin D in Winter

Between October and March, the UK doesn't receive enough UVB sunlight for vitamin D production. Public Health England recommends all adults take a 10-microgram (400 IU) vitamin D supplement daily during autumn and winter. Vitamin D is important for bone health, immune function and may help reduce arthritis-related inflammation.

Winter doesn't have to mean retreating from physical activity. With the right preparation, indoor alternatives and motivation strategies, you can stay active throughout the British winter and emerge in spring with stronger, more mobile joints. Our virtual assistant can help you create a winter exercise plan tailored to your abilities.

This article is for general information only. Consult your GP before starting a new exercise programme, particularly if you have balance problems or cardiovascular conditions.

### Practical next steps for Staying Active with Arthritis in Winter: UK Guide to Cold-Weather Exercise If you came here about **Staying Active with Arthritis in Winter: UK Guide to Cold-Weather Exercise**, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete. In many areas you can ask your primary care network about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live. ### Pacing on good and bad days On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether. ### Building a joint-friendly routine Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery. ### Peer support etiquette Share what helps you without prescribing it for others. Conditions, medicines and life circumstances differ. If someone is in crisis, encourage them toward NHS 111, their GP, or emergency services rather than relying on a forum alone. ### Quick questions about Staying Active with Arthritis **Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician?** No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team. **How long before I judge whether a change helped?** Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner. **What should I track?** Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings. ### Safety and when to get urgent help This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous. ### Keep learning with us Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis UK — try the [guides hub](/guides), [diet hub](/diet), [exercise hub](/exercises), or [site search](/search) to filter by topic and length. article.title: Strength Training with Arthritis: A Beginner's Safe Start Guide
article.excerpt: Resistance training builds the muscle support your joints need. This physiotherapist-designed programme starts gently and progresses safely.
article.content:
Quick answer: Strength training is beneficial for arthritis, reducing pain and improving function. A beginner programme could include wall push-ups, seated leg extensions, and resistance band rows for weeks 1–2. Progress to chair squats and step-ups in weeks 3–4. Always warm up, avoid training through sharp pain, and allow 48 hours rest between sessions for the same muscle group.

## Why Strength Matters\n\nStrong muscles absorb shock and stabilise joints, reducing the load on damaged cartilage. Systematic reviews in *The Lancet Rheumatology* and elsewhere consistently show that regular resistance training meaningfully reduces knee OA pain over time, which is why it is a core recommendation in NICE guidance for managing osteoarthritis.\n\n### The 4-Week Starter Programme\n\n#### Week 1–2: Foundation\n- Wall push-ups: 2 sets × 8 reps\n- Seated leg extensions: 2 sets × 10 reps\n- Standing calf raises: 2 sets × 12 reps\n- Resistance band rows: 2 sets × 8 reps\n\n#### Week 3–4: Progression\n- Chair squats: 2 sets × 10 reps\n- Resistance band chest press: 2 sets × 10 reps\n- Step-ups (low step): 2 sets × 8 per leg\n- Plank hold: 2 × 15 seconds\n\n### Golden Rules\n\n1. **Never train through sharp pain** — dull ache during exercise is acceptable\n2. **Apply the 24-hour rule**: if a joint is more swollen or painful 24 hours after exercise, you did too much\n3. **Warm up first**: 5 minutes of gentle movement\n4. **Rest days matter**: allow 48 hours between sessions for the same muscle group\n\n*Programme by Sarah Mitchell, MCSP, HCPC Registered Physiotherapist* ## What the Evidence Says Extensive high-quality research shows that regular strength training is incredibly beneficial for people living with various forms of arthritis. Systematic reviews, which combine results from many different studies, consistently find that strengthening exercises lead to significant reductions in pain, improved physical function, and a better quality of life. These benefits are seen across different joints and types of arthritis. Clinical guidelines from leading rheumatology organisations universally recommend incorporating strength training into arthritis management plans. These recommendations are based on strong evidence from randomised controlled trials, which are considered the gold standard in medical research. They show that supervised, progressive resistance exercise is not only effective but also safe when performed correctly. The improvements aren't just about feeling better; studies also indicate that strengthening muscles around arthritic joints can slow down disease progression in some cases, by stabilising the joint and helping to protect the cartilage from further wear and tear. ## Common Mistakes to Avoid * **Starting too heavy too soon:** Begin with easily manageable weights or bodyweight to establish good form. * **Holding your breath:** Breathe out during the effort part of the exercise and in during the recovery. * **Skipping warm-ups or cool-downs:** Always prepare your body and gently wind down to prevent stiffness. * **Only focusing on one muscle group:** Aim for a balanced programme that works all major muscle groups. * **Not listening to your body:** Differentiate between muscle fatigue and joint pain. If a joint hurts, stop. ## When to Speak to a Clinician While strength training is generally very safe and beneficial, there are times when it's really important to get advice from a healthcare professional. If you experience new or worsening symptoms that are beyond what you'd expect from typical muscle soreness, or if you're uncertain about how to exercise safely with your particular type of arthritis, please reach out to your doctor, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist. You should seek advice if you experience: * Sudden, severe joint pain that doesn't settle. * Increased joint swelling, redness, or warmth that lasts more than 24 hours. * New numbness, tingling, or weakness in a limb. * Pain that wakes you up at night or is present at rest. * Difficulty performing daily tasks due to exercise-related joint issues. ## Frequently Asked Questions ### How often should I lift weights if I have arthritis? For most people, two to three sessions per week targeting the major muscle groups is ideal. This allows sufficient time for muscle recovery and adaptation, which is crucial for building strength and preventing overuse. ### Can strength training make my arthritis worse? When done correctly and progressively, strength training is highly unlikely to make your arthritis worse. In fact, it typically improves symptoms. The key is to start gently, listen to your body, and never push through sharp pain, always respecting the 24-hour rule. ### Do I need to buy special equipment for strength training? Not at all! Many effective strength exercises can be done using just your body weight, such as squats, lunges, and push-ups against a wall. Resistance bands are also an excellent, affordable way to add challenge, and household items like full water bottles can serve as light weights. ### Practical next steps for Strength Training with Arthritis: A Beginner's Safe Start Guide If you came here about **Strength Training with Arthritis: A Beginner's Safe Start Guide**, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. article.title: PIP for Arthritis – How to Apply in the UK
article.excerpt: Complete UK guide to claiming Personal Independence Payment (PIP) for arthritis. Learn eligibility criteria, how to apply, assessment tips, and appeal rights.
article.content:
If arthritis significantly affects your daily life, you may be eligible for Personal Independence Payment (PIP) — a UK benefit that helps with the extra costs of living with a long-term health condition. This guide covers everything you need to know about claiming PIP for arthritis.

Quick answer: Personal Independence Payment (PIP) for arthritis is a UK benefit that helps with additional living costs due to a long-term health condition. It has Daily Living and Mobility components, each with standard and enhanced rates. Eligibility depends on how arthritis affects daily activities or movement, not solely on diagnosis. To apply, call the DWP, complete the PIP2 form, and gather evidence.

What Is PIP?

PIP is a non-means-tested benefit for people aged 16 to State Pension age. It has two components:

  • Daily Living — help with everyday tasks like preparing food, washing, dressing, and managing medications
  • Mobility — help with getting around, planning journeys, and moving safely

Each component has a standard and enhanced rate. You can receive one or both components.

Am I Eligible?

You may be eligible if arthritis affects your ability to carry out daily activities or get around. PIP is based on how your condition affects you, not on your diagnosis alone. Key considerations include:

  • Pain levels during flare-ups and on average days
  • Stiffness that limits your movement, especially in the morning
  • Fatigue that prevents you completing tasks
  • Need for aids, adaptations, or help from another person
  • Variability — even if you have good days, your worst days matter

How to Apply

  1. Call the DWP on 0800 917 2222 to start your claim
  2. Complete the PIP2 form — describe your worst days, not your best
  3. Gather evidence — GP letters, hospital reports, medication lists
  4. Attend the assessment — usually a face-to-face or telephone consultation

Tips for a Successful Claim

  • Keep a diary of how arthritis affects you over 2-4 weeks before applying
  • Describe your worst days and how often they occur
  • Mention every joint affected, every medication, and every adaptation you use
  • Ask your GP, consultant, or physiotherapist for supporting evidence
  • Contact Citizens Advice or a local welfare rights service for free help

If Your Claim Is Refused

Around 70% of PIP decisions are overturned at tribunal. If you disagree with the decision:

  1. Request a Mandatory Reconsideration within one month
  2. If still refused, appeal to a First-tier Tribunal
  3. Get free help from Citizens Advice, local law centres, or disability charities

This guide is for information purposes only and does not constitute legal or financial advice. Contact the DWP or Citizens Advice for personalised guidance.

Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete. In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live. ### Benefits conversations Personal Independence Payment (PIP) looks at how your condition affects daily living and mobility, not the diagnosis name alone. Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them. ### Work, rights and practical adjustments Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting. ### Supplements versus meals Food-first is usually safer than stacking capsules. If you do try a supplement, choose a reputable UK brand, check for interactions with your medicines (especially blood thinners), and give any trial a clear stop date so you can judge whether symptoms truly changed. ### Quick questions about Arthritis Apply **Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician?** No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team. **How long before I judge whether a change helped?** Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner. **What should I track?** Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings. ### Safety and when to get urgent help This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. article.title: TENS Machines for Arthritis UK: Do They Work and How to Use Them
article.excerpt: Complete UK guide to using TENS machines for arthritis pain. How they work, evidence for effectiveness, best devices, settings and NHS availability.
article.content:
TENS (Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation) machines are one of the most popular drug-free pain relief options for arthritis in the UK. These small, battery-powered devices deliver mild electrical impulses through electrode pads placed on the skin near painful joints. With prices starting from just £15 and no prescription needed, TENS machines are accessible and widely used — but do they actually work for arthritis? This guide examines the evidence, explains how to use one effectively and helps you choose the right device.

Quick answer: TENS machines are drug-free devices that deliver mild electrical impulses through pads on the skin, a popular choice for arthritis pain relief. They work by stimulating nerves to "close the gate" on pain signals (high frequency, 80-120 Hz) and by triggering endorphin release (low frequency, 2-5 Hz). Evidence suggests short-term pain relief, but they are best used as part of a wider pain management plan.

How TENS Works

TENS machines work through two main mechanisms:

Gate Control Theory

At high frequencies (80–120 Hz), TENS stimulates large nerve fibres that "close the gate" on pain signals travelling to the brain. Essentially, the tingling sensation from the TENS overrides the pain signals, reducing your perception of pain. This is similar to rubbing a bumped elbow — the pressure sensation partially blocks the pain signal.

Endorphin Release

At lower frequencies (2–5 Hz), TENS triggers the release of endorphins — the body's natural painkillers. This takes longer to work (20–30 minutes) but the pain relief can last longer after the device is switched off.

What the Evidence Says

The evidence for TENS in arthritis is mixed but generally positive for short-term pain relief:

  • A Cochrane review of TENS for knee osteoarthritis found some evidence of pain reduction, though study quality was variable
  • A meta-analysis in Physiotherapy found TENS provided statistically significant pain relief for OA compared to placebo
  • NICE acknowledges TENS as an option for osteoarthritis pain management alongside other treatments
  • Many rheumatology and physiotherapy departments in the UK recommend TENS as part of multimodal pain management
  • Patient satisfaction is generally high — many users report meaningful pain relief even when clinical trial results are modest

TENS is best viewed as one tool in a pain management toolkit, not a standalone treatment. It works well alongside exercise, medication and other approaches.

How to Use a TENS Machine for Arthritis

Pad Placement

Correct electrode placement is crucial for effective pain relief:

  • Knee arthritis — Place two pads on either side of the kneecap, or one above and one below the joint
  • Hip arthritis — Place pads around the hip joint — one at the front, one at the side or back
  • Hand/wrist arthritis — Use smaller pads on either side of the painful joint
  • Shoulder arthritis — Place pads on the front and back of the shoulder, or above and below the joint
  • Spine/back arthritis — Place pads on either side of the spine at the painful level (never directly on the spine)

Settings

  • Start with a high frequency (80–100 Hz) for immediate tingling pain relief
  • Try low frequency (2–5 Hz) for deeper, endorphin-based relief
  • Increase intensity gradually until you feel a strong but comfortable tingling — it should never be painful
  • Use for 20–60 minutes per session, up to several times daily
  • Experiment with settings — what works varies between individuals

Tips for Best Results

  • Clean and dry the skin before applying pads
  • Don't place pads on broken skin, over varicose veins or near the front of the neck
  • Replace electrode pads when they lose stickiness (every 20–30 uses typically)
  • Use during activities that usually cause pain (walking, gardening, housework)
  • Try using TENS before exercise to enable more comfortable movement

Choosing a TENS Machine

Key features to consider:

  • Dual channel — Allows you to use 4 pads simultaneously for larger areas or multiple joints
  • Adjustable frequency and intensity — More control over settings for optimal relief
  • Rechargeable battery — More economical than disposable batteries
  • Pre-set programmes — Useful for beginners, with settings optimised for different pain types
  • Timer — Automatic shut-off prevents overuse

Where to Buy in the UK

  • Boots, Superdrug and Lloyds Pharmacy stock TENS machines (from £15)
  • Amazon and online retailers offer a wide range
  • Physiotherapy suppliers (e.g., TensCare, Beurer) for more advanced devices
  • Some NHS physiotherapy departments loan TENS machines for trial periods — ask your physiotherapist

Who Should Not Use TENS

  • People with pacemakers or other implanted electrical devices (unless approved by cardiologist)
  • During pregnancy (certain pad placements)
  • Over areas of reduced sensation (neuropathy)
  • On active cancer sites
  • While driving or operating machinery

TENS machines are a safe, affordable and drug-free option for arthritis pain relief. While they don't work for everyone, many people find them a valuable addition to their pain management routine. Our virtual assistant can help you with pad placement guidance for your specific joints.

This article is for general information only. Consult your GP or physiotherapist if you're unsure whether TENS is suitable for you.
