article.title: Expert Q&A: When to Consider Spinal Injections vs Exercise
article.excerpt: Exercise is first-line for chronic back arthritis. Injections are reserved for severe flares unresponsive to 12 weeks of structured therapy. What to expect.
article.content:
Quick answer: The post says arthritis-related spinal or joint pain should be managed by identifying inflammatory or degenerative patterns. It presents structured movement and graded exercise as first-line, supported by diet, weight management, heat or cold, sleep routines and small weekly goals. It advises GP or physiotherapy review for hot swollen joints, weight loss, prolonged morning stiffness, numbness or weakness.

## What this guide covers This piece summarises what the current evidence says about **expert q&a: when to consider spinal injections vs exercise**, the practical steps that help most, and the red flags that mean you should speak to your GP or physiotherapist. It is written for people living in the UK and reviewed by our clinical team. ## The underlying mechanism Arthritis pain rarely has a single cause. Joint cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, surrounding muscle and the nervous system all contribute. Understanding which of these is driving your specific symptom is the first step toward targeted relief. For an in-depth condition overview, see our [related guide](/conditions/ankylosing-spondylitis/treatment). Inflammatory and degenerative forms behave differently. Inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid, psoriatic, ankylosing spondylitis) typically worsens with rest and improves with gentle movement. Degenerative arthritis (osteoarthritis) typically worsens with prolonged use. Knowing which pattern matches your day-to-day experience helps you choose the right management approach. ## What helps — by strength of evidence 1. **Movement and graded exercise.** NICE NG226 (2022) and Cochrane reviews place structured exercise as a first-line treatment. Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, split into 20–30 minute sessions. 2. **Anti-inflammatory eating.** A Mediterranean-style pattern — oily fish twice a week, plenty of vegetables, olive oil, whole grains — is linked to reduced pain scores in OA and RA trials. 3. **Weight management.** A 5 percent reduction in body weight reduces knee-OA symptoms measurably; a 10 percent reduction can match the effect of some medications. 4. **Heat and cold.** Heat eases stiffness; cold eases acute swelling. Twenty-minute applications, with a towel barrier. 5. **Sleep hygiene.** Pain perception rises sharply on fewer than six hours of sleep. Prioritise a consistent bedtime. ## A practical seven-day starting plan Begin with the smallest dose that feels manageable — five minutes of movement, one anti-inflammatory meal a day, a 10 pm screen-off rule. Track only three things weekly: pain on waking (0–10), longest pain-free interval, and one functional win (e.g., climbed stairs without grabbing the rail). Small, consistent inputs outperform big sporadic efforts. ## When to seek clinical advice Book an appointment with your GP or a first-contact physiotherapist if you notice: sudden hot, red, swollen joints; unexplained weight loss alongside joint pain; morning stiffness lasting longer than an hour for more than two weeks; or new numbness or weakness. These can signal inflammatory disease that benefits from early treatment. ## Frequently asked questions **Will this approach work alongside my medication?** Yes. Exercise, diet and pacing complement prescribed treatments and often improve their effectiveness. Always check with your prescriber before stopping any medication. **How long until I notice a difference?** Most people report meaningful improvement at 6–12 weeks of consistent practice. Earlier wins (less morning stiffness, better sleep) often appear within 2–3 weeks. **Is this safe if I have other conditions?** The principles above are broadly safe for adults with stable cardiovascular, metabolic and respiratory conditions. If you are unsure, ask your GP for a referral to a first-contact physiotherapist for a tailored plan. --- *This article is general health information, not medical advice. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether. ### Building a joint-friendly routine Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery. ### Preparing for appointments Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. article.content:
Best yoga poses for ankylosing spondylitis stiffness — AS causes progressive spinal stiffness and can severely limit mobility over time. Yoga, when correctly adapted, is one of the best tools available for maintaining spinal mobility, reducing stiffness and managing pain in AS.

Quick answer: Best yoga poses for AS stiffness: cat-cow for spinal mobility, sphinx pose for gentle extension, supine spinal twist for rotation, child's pose for thoracic stretch, standing chest opener for rib cage. Avoid deep forward folds. Practice 1-2 hours after morning medication when stiffness has eased.

Why Yoga Specifically Helps AS

NICE guidelines recommend regular exercise, particularly exercises that promote spinal extension and rotation, as a cornerstone of AS management. Yoga provides systematic movement through the spine, hips and chest — exactly the areas where AS causes stiffness. A 2019 RCT found 12 weeks of yoga practice significantly improved spinal mobility, pain scores and quality of life in AS patients compared to a control group.

Recommended Poses for AS

Cat-Cow (Marjaryasana-Bitilasana)

On hands and knees. Inhale: arch back downward, lift head and tailbone (cow). Exhale: round spine upward, tuck chin and pelvis (cat). 10 slow repetitions. Gently mobilises the entire spine in flexion and extension.

Sphinx Pose (Salamba Bhujangasana)

Lie face down, forearms on the floor, elbows under shoulders. Press forearms gently to lift chest slightly. Hold 30–60 seconds. Gentle spinal extension that counteracts the forward-bending tendency of AS.

Supine Spinal Twist

Lie on back. Draw one knee to chest, then guide it across to the opposite side while extending that arm wide. Hold 30 seconds each side. Gentle thoracic and lumbar rotation.

Spinal mobility exercises — openly licensed via Openverse

Child's Pose (Balasana) — Modified

From kneeling, slowly lower hips toward heels and stretch arms forward. If hips do not reach heels, place a folded blanket between thighs and calves. Gently stretches thoracic spine and hips.

Standing Chest Opener

Stand in doorway, arms at 90 degrees on the frame. Lean forward gently until chest stretch is felt. Hold 20–30 seconds. Opens the anterior chest and rib cage — important in AS where chest expansion can be restricted.

AS-Specific Adaptations

  • Always warm up for 10 minutes before starting
  • Avoid deep forward folds — these can load already-fused or vulnerable spinal segments
  • Use props freely: blocks, bolsters, straps — they make poses accessible, not easier
  • Practice in the morning after medication has taken effect (typically 1–2 hours after taking NSAIDs)
  • Tell your yoga teacher about your AS before class — a good teacher will modify accordingly

Short answer: Very gentle movement (cat-cow, supine twist) is generally safe during mild flares. Avoid new poses or increased intensity during severe flares. Resume gradually as the flare settles.

article.title: How to Manage Fibromyalgia Flare Ups Without Medication
article.excerpt: Practical, evidence-based strategies for managing fibromyalgia flare ups without increasing medication — pacing, sleep, heat, movement and mind-body approaches.
article.content:
How to manage fibromyalgia flare ups without medication is a question that reflects a real need — many people with fibromyalgia want to manage their worst periods through self-management, either to avoid medication side effects or because current medication is not providing enough relief.

Quick answer: Managing fibromyalgia flare ups without medication: pace activity (reduce but do not stop), apply heat to painful muscle areas, maintain minimal movement (5-10 min walks), prioritise sleep hygiene. Avoid boom-bust cycles. A symptom diary helps identify personal triggers.

Mobility support during flares — openly licensed via Openverse

Understanding Fibromyalgia Flares

A fibromyalgia flare is a period of significantly increased pain, fatigue, cognitive difficulties ("brain fog") and often disturbed sleep. Flares can be triggered by overexertion, stress, sleep disruption, illness, weather changes or — frustratingly — no identifiable cause at all. Understanding your personal triggers through a symptom diary is the first step in management.

Pacing: The Foundation of Flare Management

Pacing means matching activity level to your current energy and pain level, rather than pushing through when symptoms are high (the "boom-bust" cycle). During a flare:

  • Reduce activities to your current sustainable level — not zero, but significantly less than baseline
  • Break tasks into small chunks with rest periods between
  • Prioritise — what must be done today? What can wait?
  • Accept the temporary reduction without self-blame

Rest and support during flares — openly licensed via Openverse

Heat Therapy

Heat is one of the most immediately effective non-pharmacological pain relievers for fibromyalgia. It increases blood flow, relaxes muscle tension and reduces pain signal transmission. During a flare: hot bath or shower (15–20 minutes), heated blanket over painful areas, warm wheat bag or heat pad on tender muscle groups. Avoid heat on any inflamed joints — for fibromyalgia's diffuse muscle pain, heat is safe and effective.

Gentle Movement

Complete rest during a flare is counterproductive — it worsens deconditioning and can extend the flare. Aim for minimal but consistent movement: 5–10 minute gentle walks if possible, chair-based stretching, or even just standing briefly every 30–60 minutes. Movement helps reset the central sensitisation that underlies fibromyalgia pain.

Sleep Hygiene

Disturbed sleep worsens fibromyalgia pain and fatigue significantly. During flares prioritise: consistent sleep/wake time, dark and cool bedroom, avoiding screens 60 minutes before bed, and a brief relaxation practice (body scan, slow breathing) before sleep.

Question: How long does a fibromyalgia flare typically last?
Short answer: This varies enormously. Minor flares may last 2–3 days; major flares can last 2–4 weeks. Consistent application of pacing, sleep and heat strategies typically shortens duration.

Question: Should I see my GP during a flare?
Short answer: If the flare is significantly worse than usual, has a clear new trigger (illness, injury), involves fever or new symptoms, contact your GP. Quick answer: The article says arthritis pain can come from several joint and nervous system factors, so matching inflammatory or degenerative patterns matters. It presents structured exercise as first-line, with Mediterranean-style eating including oily fish, weight management, heat or cold, and sleep hygiene as helpful. It advises small weekly tracking and GP or physiotherapist review for red flags.

## What this guide covers This piece summarises what the current evidence says about **fatty fish and omega-3s: the evidence for arthritis pain**, the practical steps that help most, and the red flags that mean you should speak to your GP or physiotherapist. It is written for people living in the UK and reviewed by our clinical team. ## The underlying mechanism Arthritis pain rarely has a single cause. Joint cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, surrounding muscle and the nervous system all contribute. Understanding which of these is driving your specific symptom is the first step toward targeted relief. For an in-depth condition overview, see our [related guide](/diet). Inflammatory and degenerative forms behave differently. Inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid, psoriatic, ankylosing spondylitis) typically worsens with rest and improves with gentle movement. Degenerative arthritis (osteoarthritis) typically worsens with prolonged use. Knowing which pattern matches your day-to-day experience helps you choose the right management approach. ## What helps — by strength of evidence 1. **Movement and graded exercise.** NICE NG226 (2022) and Cochrane reviews place structured exercise as a first-line treatment. Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, split into 20–30 minute sessions. 2. **Anti-inflammatory eating.** A Mediterranean-style pattern — oily fish twice a week, plenty of vegetables, olive oil, whole grains — is linked to reduced pain scores in OA and RA trials. 3. **Weight management.** A 5 percent reduction in body weight reduces knee-OA symptoms measurably; a 10 percent reduction can match the effect of some medications. 4. **Heat and cold.** Heat eases stiffness; cold eases acute swelling. Twenty-minute applications, with a towel barrier. 5. **Sleep hygiene.** Pain perception rises sharply on fewer than six hours of sleep. Prioritise a consistent bedtime. ## A practical seven-day starting plan Begin with the smallest dose that feels manageable — five minutes of movement, one anti-inflammatory meal a day, a 10 pm screen-off rule. Track only three things weekly: pain on waking (0–10), longest pain-free interval, and one functional win (e.g., climbed stairs without grabbing the rail). Small, consistent inputs outperform big sporadic efforts. ## When to seek clinical advice Book an appointment with your GP or a first-contact physiotherapist if you notice: sudden hot, red, swollen joints; unexplained weight loss alongside joint pain; morning stiffness lasting longer than an hour for more than two weeks; or new numbness or weakness. These can signal inflammatory disease that benefits from early treatment. ## Frequently asked questions **Will this approach work alongside my medication?** Yes. Exercise, diet and pacing complement prescribed treatments and often improve their effectiveness. Always check with your prescriber before stopping any medication. **How long until I notice a difference?** Most people report meaningful improvement at 6–12 weeks of consistent practice. Earlier wins (less morning stiffness, better sleep) often appear within 2–3 weeks. **Is this safe if I have other conditions?** The principles above are broadly safe for adults with stable cardiovascular, metabolic and respiratory conditions. If you are unsure, ask your GP for a referral to a first-contact physiotherapist for a tailored plan. --- *This article is general health information, not medical advice. article.title: Hip Replacement Recovery Week by Week
article.excerpt: A realistic 12-week timeline most people follow.
article.content:
Quick answer: After hip replacement, most people gradually reduce walking aid reliance over 2-6 weeks. Driving may resume around 6 weeks, depending on comfort and being able to perform an emergency stop. Low-impact activities are often possible within 6-12 weeks, while more demanding hobbies can take 3-6 months. High-impact sports are generally not recommended.

## Overview A realistic 12-week timeline most people follow. ## What the evidence shows UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Versus Arthritis consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus. ## What this means for you - **Talk to your clinician.** Personalised advice always beats blanket rules. - **Track your symptoms.** Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days. - **Move within comfort.** Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood. - **Watch the warning signs.** New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review. ## Practical next steps 1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: [related guidance](/exercises/hip). 2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment. 3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day. ## Editorial standards This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis Editorial Team and reviewed by our Clinical Review Board against UK NICE guidance and peer-reviewed sources. We update content at least annually. ## What the Evidence Says Large-scale reviews of medical studies consistently show that hip replacement surgery significantly improves pain and mobility for most people with severe hip arthritis. These reviews, which combine data from many individual trials, highlight the long-term effectiveness of the procedure. Clinical guidelines from leading UK bodies support hip replacement as a highly successful treatment option when non-surgical approaches are no longer effective. The evidence also strongly emphasises the importance of rehabilitation after surgery. Systematic reviews demonstrate that a structured exercise programme, often with input from a physiotherapist, leads to better recovery outcomes, including improved walking ability and greater strength. While individual results vary, consistent participation in your prescribed exercises is key to regaining full function. Furthermore, research indicates that educating patients about what to expect during recovery, including potential challenges and milestones, can significantly reduce anxiety and improve satisfaction with the overall experience. This patient education, combined with strong support from family and healthcare professionals, contributes to a more positive and successful recovery journey. ## Common Mistakes to Avoid * **Doing too much too soon:** Thinking you're fully recovered early on and overdoing activities. *Listen to your body and stick to your exercise plan without rushing.* * **Neglecting exercises:** Skipping your prescribed physiotherapy exercises because you feel well or are busy. *These exercises are crucial for strength and flexibility; make them a daily priority.* * **Ignoring pain signals:** Pushing through sharp or increasing pain, believing it's a necessary part of recovery. *Differentiate between muscle soreness and warning signs; consult your physiotherapist if pain is worsening.* * **Poor posture and movement habits:** Falling back into old ways of moving that put strain on your hip. *Be mindful of your posture and gait, especially when sitting or lifting.* * **Expecting immediate perfection:** Becoming disheartened if progress isn't perfectly linear or as fast as you hoped. *Recovery is a journey with ups and downs; celebrate small victories.* ## When to Speak to a Clinician While some discomfort and swelling are normal after hip replacement surgery, specific symptoms warrant prompt attention from your GP, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist. It's important not to delay if you experience any of these red flags, as early intervention can prevent complications and support your recovery. Your healthcare team is there to help guide you safely through this process. * Sudden, severe pain in your hip or leg that isn't eased by rest or medication. * New or increasing redness, warmth, or discharge around your incision site. * Fever (a temperature of 38°C or higher) accompanied by chills. * Significant, unexplained swelling in your operated leg, particularly if only in one leg. * Sudden difficulty bearing weight or a noticeable change in your leg length. * Shortness of breath or chest pain. ## Frequently Asked Questions ### How long until I can walk without crutches? Most people gradually reduce their reliance on walking aids over the first 2-6 weeks after surgery. Your physiotherapist will guide you on when it's safe to progress, depending on your strength and stability. It's important not to rush this process to prevent falls and allow proper healing. ### Can I drive after a hip replacement? Generally, you can start driving again once you can comfortably get in and out of the car, operate the pedals safely (especially if it's your right hip), and perform an emergency stop without pain. This typically takes around 6 weeks, but your surgeon will give you specific advice. Always check with your insurance provider too. ### When can I return to my usual activities and hobbies? Low-impact activities like swimming, cycling on a stationary bike, and walking can often be resumed within 6-12 weeks, as advised by your physiotherapist. More demanding activities, such as gardening, golf, or dancing, might take 3-6 months. High-impact sports are generally not recommended after a hip replacement to protect the joint. ### Practical next steps for Hip Replacement Recovery Week by Week If you came here about **Hip Replacement Recovery Week by Week**, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete. In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live. ### Working with NHS pathways Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates. ### Working with NHS pathways Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates. ### Everyday eating patterns No single food cures arthritis. Patterns rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses, wholegrains and oily fish are the ones most often discussed in UK dietetic advice for inflammatory conditions. Keep changes realistic: swap one ultra-processed snack for fruit and nuts, or cook with olive oil more often than seed oils marketed as miracle cures. ### Quick questions about Replacement Recovery Week Week **Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician?** No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team. **How long before I judge whether a change helped?** Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner. **What should I track?** Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. article.excerpt: Practical, compassionate guidance for supporting a friend through a new lupus diagnosis — what to say, what to do and what to avoid.
article.content:
A new lupus diagnosis is frightening and often isolating. Your support as a friend can make an enormous difference — but knowing how to help effectively, without overstepping or inadvertently minimising what your friend is going through, takes thought.

Quick answer: To support a friend with new lupus: offer specific practical help, learn the basics of lupus, be flexible with plans (flares are unpredictable), avoid minimising phrases like "you look well." Lupus UK helpline: 01708 731251.

Friendship and support — openly licensed via Openverse

What Lupus Actually Involves

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks the body's own tissues. It causes joint pain, fatigue, skin rashes (including the characteristic butterfly rash across the cheeks), and can affect internal organs including kidneys, heart and lungs. It is unpredictable — your friend may look fine one week and be unable to function the next. This variability is one of the hardest things for outsiders to understand.

What to Say (and What Not to Say)

Helpful

  • "I'm here for you — what would be most useful right now?"
  • "Would you like me to come with you to an appointment?"
  • "Tell me what a bad day looks like so I can understand better."
  • "I'm bringing dinner on Tuesday — what time works?"

Unhelpful (avoid these)

  • "But you look so well!" — invalidates invisible symptoms
  • "Have you tried [unproven remedy]?" — implies they should be doing more
  • "At least it's not cancer" — minimises a serious chronic condition
  • "You just need to think more positively" — oversimplifies a complex illness

Community and friendship — openly licensed via Openverse

Practical Things You Can Do

  • Offer specific, scheduled help — "I'll pick up your prescription on Thursday" is more useful than "let me know if you need anything."
  • Learn the basics of lupus — understanding what triggers flares and what symptoms to watch for shows you take it seriously.
  • Be flexible with plans — lupus flares are unpredictable. Adopting a "no hard feelings" approach to cancelled plans reduces your friend's anxiety and guilt.
  • Check in regularly without pressure — a simple "how are you today, no need to reply at length" message can mean a lot.

Question: My friend seems angry and withdrawn since diagnosis — is this normal?
Short answer: Yes. Anger, grief, fear and withdrawal are all normal responses to a significant chronic illness diagnosis. Give your friend space while making clear your support is available whenever they want it.

article.title: Chair Yoga for Elderly Arthritis Stiffness Beginners
article.excerpt: A complete beginner's guide to chair yoga for elderly people with arthritis stiffness — safe, seated poses that improve mobility, balance and confidence.
article.content:
Chair yoga for elderly arthritis stiffness beginners is one of the most accessible and effective approaches to maintaining mobility in later life. By using a sturdy chair for support, chair yoga makes the benefits of yoga available to people who cannot comfortably get up and down from the floor.

Quick answer: Chair yoga for elderly arthritis: seated cat-cow, shoulder rolls, ankle circles, seated forward fold, seated twist and chair pigeon pose. Practise 15-20 minutes daily or 3-4x/week. Uses a sturdy chair for support. Clinical trial evidence confirms benefits for pain, fatigue and balance in OA.

Chair-based exercise — openly licensed via Openverse

Evidence for Chair Yoga in Older Adults

A 2017 randomised controlled trial published in JAMDA found chair yoga significantly reduced pain and fatigue, and improved gait speed, in older adults with OA. Multiple reviews confirm chair yoga is safe and effective for improving balance, flexibility and reducing fall risk in adults over 65.

The Basic Chair Yoga Session (20 Minutes)

Warm-Up (5 minutes)

  • Seated cat-cow: Sit upright, hands on knees. Inhale and arch back, lifting chest (cow). Exhale and round spine forward (cat). 8 repetitions.
  • Shoulder rolls: Roll shoulders forward 5 times, then backward 5 times. Releases shoulder and neck tension.
  • Seated ankle circles: Lift one foot slightly, circle ankle 8 times each direction. Repeat other side. Improves ankle mobility and circulation.

Main Poses (10 minutes)

  • Seated mountain pose: Sit tall, feet flat, hands on thighs. Take 5 slow deep breaths. Establishes posture awareness.
  • Seated forward fold: Feet flat, hinge forward from hips (not waist), letting hands rest on shins. Hold 30 seconds. Gently stretches lower back.
  • Seated twist: Place right hand on left knee, left hand on chair back. Gently twist left. Hold 20 seconds. Repeat other side. Mobilises thoracic spine.
  • Chair pigeon: Cross right ankle over left knee. Sit tall. Hold 30 seconds each side. Stretches hip external rotators — tight in most people with hip OA.

Gentle group movement — openly licensed via Openverse

Cool-Down (5 minutes)

  • Seated breathing — slow, deep breaths, 5 counts in, 7 counts out. Activates parasympathetic nervous system and reduces pain perception.

Safety Guidelines

  • Use a solid, non-wheeled chair placed against a wall if needed
  • Move slowly and breathe throughout — never hold breath during effort
  • Stop if you feel sharp or shooting pain
  • Stay within a comfortable range — no forcing

Short answer: Daily sessions of 15–20 minutes are ideal. Even 3–4 times per week produces measurable improvement in stiffness and balance within 4–6 weeks.

article.title: How to Claim PIP for Osteoarthritis in Both Knees
article.excerpt: A practical guide to claiming PIP when you have osteoarthritis in both knees — how to describe functional impact and maximise your application.
article.content:
How to claim PIP for osteoarthritis in both knees — bilateral knee OA can severely limit mobility and daily activities, but because it is not immediately visible and many people with OA push through pain without complaint, PIP applications for OA are often initially refused. This guide shows you how to claim effectively.

Quick answer: For PIP with bilateral knee OA: describe functional impact in detail — standing time limit, difficulty dressing, mobility distance with stops. Include GP supporting letter stating functional limitations (not just diagnosis). An OT assessment report is strong evidence. If refused, appeal — 60-70% success rate at tribunal.

Knee osteoarthritis — openly licensed via Openverse

Does OA in Both Knees Qualify for PIP?

Yes — if it substantially affects your daily living or mobility activities. The DWP does not award PIP based on a diagnosis. A successful claim depends on clearly describing how OA in both knees affects you on your worst typical days (which, for bilateral severe OA, might mean most days).

Daily Living Activities Commonly Affected by Bilateral Knee OA

  • Preparing food: Cannot stand at the hob for more than 10 minutes without significant pain
  • Washing and bathing: Cannot get in/out of bath unaided; needs grab rail or walk-in shower
  • Dressing: Cannot pull on trousers or socks without difficulty due to limited knee bend
  • Managing medication: Opens bottles with difficulty; needs blister pack dispensing

Severe knee OA — openly licensed via Openverse

Mobility Activities Affected

  • Moving around: Cannot walk 20 metres without stopping due to pain; uses a stick; avoids uneven ground
  • Planning and following journeys: Cannot use public transport without assistance due to steps; cannot walk from car park distances

Key Application Tips

  1. Describe your worst typical days — not your best days or how you manage with considerable effort
  2. Include: pain levels on a 0–10 scale, what happens when you walk further than your limit, how long recovery takes after exertion
  3. Get a supporting letter from your GP stating functional limitations specifically (not just diagnosis)
  4. Ask your GP about an OT referral — an OT's functional assessment report is powerful evidence

Question: I manage to walk to the shops on good days — will this count against me?
Short answer: PIP considers variability. If you can walk to shops on good days but not on the majority of days, describe both scenarios. The DWP is supposed to consider your experience across all days.

Question: I was refused PIP for my knees last year — can I apply again?
Short answer: Yes. You can reapply if your circumstances have changed (worsened), if your previous application was poorly evidenced, or if significant time has passed. article.title: How to Manage Arthritis Pain Flare Ups at Night
article.excerpt: Practical strategies to manage arthritis pain and flare ups at night — mattress, position, medication timing and sleep techniques.
article.content:
Night-time arthritis pain is one of the most disruptive symptoms of the condition — disrupted sleep worsens pain sensitivity, fatigue and mood the following day, creating a vicious cycle. This guide breaks that cycle with evidence-based strategies.

Quick answer: Manage arthritis pain at night: time slow-release NSAIDs in the evening (discuss with GP), use supportive pillow positioning, take a warm bath 60-90 minutes before bed, keep bedroom cool. Resting hand splints help RA morning stiffness. Night pain worsened by cortisol's overnight low.

Arthritis pain management — openly licensed via Openverse

Why Arthritis Is Often Worse at Night

Several mechanisms drive night-time arthritis pain. Cortisol (a natural anti-inflammatory hormone) drops to its lowest level overnight, removing a degree of natural inflammation suppression. Joint fluid can pool in certain positions. Inflammatory types (RA, PsA) have natural circadian rhythms — inflammation peaks in the early morning hours, which is why both night pain and morning stiffness are characteristic features.

Medication Timing

If you take NSAIDs or analgesics, timing matters. Taking a slow-release NSAID (e.g. naproxen modified release) in the evening means peak blood levels coincide with the overnight inflammatory peak. Discuss this timing adjustment with your GP or pharmacist — it can make a significant difference to sleep quality.

Rest and recovery — openly licensed via Openverse

Sleep Position and Bed Setup

  • Knee OA: A pillow between the knees when side-lying reduces hip adduction and medial knee load. A small pillow under the knees when lying flat can reduce extension stress.
  • Hip OA: Side-lying on the less affected side with a body pillow for support.
  • RA (hands): Resting hand splints worn overnight reduce morning stiffness and joint loading during sleep.
  • Mattress: Medium-firm mattress provides spinal support without pressure points. Memory foam can help distribute weight. Avoid very soft mattresses that allow excessive spinal flexion.

Pre-Sleep Strategies

  • Warm bath or shower 60–90 minutes before bed — raises core temperature, which then drops, triggering sleep onset while providing muscle relaxation
  • Gentle stretching programme of 5–10 minutes
  • Keep bedroom cool (16–18°C) — core temperature drop facilitates sleep
  • Avoid screens 60 minutes before bed

Rest and support — openly licensed via Openverse

Question: Should I use heat or cold at night for arthritis pain?
Short answer: Heat (heated blanket, wheat bag) is generally better for muscle stiffness and OA pain at night. Cold is more appropriate for acutely swollen inflammatory joints. Never apply ice directly to skin.

Question: Night pain is stopping me sleeping — when should I see my GP?
Short answer: If night pain is regularly disturbing your sleep for more than 2 weeks despite these measures, discuss with your GP. article.title: How to Find an NHS Rheumatologist Near Me Northern Ireland
article.excerpt: A practical guide to finding and accessing NHS rheumatology services in Northern Ireland — referral routes, waiting times and what to expect.
article.content:
How to find an NHS rheumatologist near me in Northern Ireland — rheumatology services in Northern Ireland are provided through the five Health and Social Care (HSC) Trusts. Unlike England, there is currently no direct self-referral pathway for rheumatology — all referrals go through your GP.

Quick answer: NHS rheumatology in Northern Ireland: ask your GP to refer you to your nearest HSC Trust rheumatology department. Current waiting times are 12-24+ months for routine; urgent (new inflammatory arthritis) should be within weeks. Patient Client Council: 0800 917 0222 for waiting list rights.

Specialist assessment — openly licensed via Openverse

The Five HSC Trust Rheumatology Departments

  • Belfast HSC Trust: Royal Victoria Hospital and Musgrave Park Hospital — the largest rheumatology centre in NI
  • Southern HSC Trust: Craigavon Area Hospital
  • South Eastern HSC Trust: Ulster Hospital, Dundonald
  • Northern HSC Trust: Antrim Area Hospital
  • Western HSC Trust: Altnagelvin Hospital, Derry/Londonderry

How to Get a Referral

Make an appointment with your GP and specifically request a rheumatology referral. NICE guidance recommends urgent referral within 3 working days for suspected new inflammatory arthritis. For established arthritis needing specialist review, routine referral is standard. Ask your GP to document that you have requested the referral and the clinical reason.

Arthritis consultation — openly licensed via Openverse

Waiting Times in NI

Northern Ireland has faced some of the longest NHS waiting times in the UK. As of 2026, routine rheumatology waits of 12–24+ months are reported. Urgent referrals should be seen faster — within weeks. If you have been waiting over 12 months without an appointment, contact the Patient Client Council (0800 917 0222) who can advise on your rights.

While You Are Waiting

  • Ask your GP to manage symptoms in the interim — NSAIDs, analgesics and physiotherapy referral can be arranged while waiting
  • Consider a private rheumatology consultation (£200–350 one-off) for a diagnosis and initial management plan
  • Contact Versus Arthritis NI (versusarthritis.org) for peer support

Health services support — openly licensed via Openverse

Q&A

Question: Can I choose which HSC Trust I am referred to?
Short answer: In Northern Ireland, choice of provider is more limited than in England. Your GP will usually refer to your nearest trust. You can ask about referral to a different trust if there are clinical reasons or significantly different wait times.

Question: What should I bring to my first rheumatology appointment?
Short answer: Full medication list, symptom diary (2–4 weeks minimum), blood test results your GP has already done, and a written list of your questions. ### Practical next steps for How to Find an NHS Rheumatologist Near Me Northern Ireland If you came here about **How to Find an NHS Rheumatologist Near Me Northern Ireland**, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. article.title: Early Signs of Gout in the Big Toe UK
article.excerpt: Recognising the early signs of gout in the big toe — what it feels like, how to confirm diagnosis and what to do at first attack.
article.content:
Early signs of gout in the big toe UK — the big toe is the most common site for a first gout attack, affecting around 70% of people at some point in their gout history. The medical term for gout in the big toe is podagra. Recognising it early helps you get the right treatment faster and prevents the attack from becoming more severe.

Quick answer: Early gout in the big toe: intense pain developing over 6-12 hours, joint becomes exquisitely tender (even sheet weight intolerable), swells, turns red and hot. See GP urgently — prescription NSAIDs or colchicine reduce severity. Apply ice, rest, elevate, drink plenty of water.

Joint inflammation — openly licensed via Openverse

What Early Gout in the Big Toe Feels Like

Gout often strikes with little warning. The early signs typically develop over 6–12 hours:

  • Intense pain: Often described as the worst pain ever experienced. The big toe MTP joint (where the toe meets the foot) becomes exquisitely tender — even the weight of a bed sheet can be intolerable.
  • Swelling: The joint and surrounding skin visibly swell within hours of the attack starting.
  • Redness and warmth: The skin over the joint turns red, shiny and hot to the touch — sometimes mistaken for an infection.
  • Peak within 12–24 hours: An untreated attack peaks within a day and then gradually resolves over 3–10 days, though the joint may remain sensitive for 2–3 weeks.

Joint inflammation — openly licensed via Openverse

Confirming the Diagnosis

See your GP as soon as possible during an attack. A blood test measuring uric acid levels supports the diagnosis — though levels can temporarily normalise during an acute attack, so a follow-up test 4 weeks later is more reliable. Your GP may also aspirate fluid from the joint (arthrocentesis) to look for urate crystals — this is the definitive diagnostic test but is not always necessary for a first attack with classic presentation.

What to Do During the First Attack

  1. See your GP or urgent care — prescription anti-inflammatories (naproxen, indomethacin) or colchicine significantly reduce attack severity and duration
  2. Rest and elevate the foot
  3. Apply ice wrapped in a cloth (15 minutes on, 15 off) — reduces inflammation and pain
  4. Stay well hydrated — aim for 2–3 litres of water daily
  5. Avoid alcohol during the attack

Question: How do I know it is gout and not an infection?
Short answer: Septic arthritis (joint infection) can look similar — both cause a hot, swollen, red, painful joint. If you also have fever or feel systemically unwell, attend A&E immediately as septic arthritis is a medical emergency.

Question: Will gout come back?
Short answer: Without treatment, gout almost always recurs — 60% of people have a second attack within 1 year. article.title: Expert Q&A: Will My Children Inherit My Arthritis?
article.excerpt: Genetics, risk and what really raises a child's odds.
article.content:
Quick answer: Children do not usually inherit arthritis in a simple, direct way. Some types, including rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis, have a genetic component, so a close relative can slightly raise susceptibility, but most children will not develop it. Genes interact with triggers such as lifestyle, infections and environment. Seek medical advice for persistent joint symptoms.

## Overview Genetics, risk and what really raises a child's odds. ## What the evidence shows UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Versus Arthritis consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus. ## What this means for you - **Talk to your clinician.** Personalised advice always beats blanket rules. - **Track your symptoms.** Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days. - **Move within comfort.** Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood. - **Watch the warning signs.** New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review. ## Practical next steps 1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: [related guidance](/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis). 2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment. 3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day. ## Editorial standards This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis Editorial Team and reviewed by our Clinical Review Board against UK NICE guidance and peer-reviewed sources. We update content at least annually. ## What the Evidence Says Current understanding from systematic reviews and clinical guidelines points to a complex picture when it comes to the inheritance of arthritis. While certain types of arthritis, like rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis, have a genetic component, it's rarely a simple case of direct inheritance. Instead, what children inherit is a predisposition or increased susceptibility. This means that while genes might load the gun, environmental factors often pull the trigger. Large population studies have helped identify specific genes linked to a higher risk, but these genes are common in the general population, and most people with them will never develop arthritis. This highlights that lifestyle, infections, and other external factors play a crucial role. The evidence consistently shows that having a close relative with certain types of arthritis increases a child’s risk factor, but this risk is still relatively small in most cases. It's more about a combination of many genes working together, alongside those environmental triggers, rather than a single 'arthritis gene' being passed down. ## Common Mistakes to Avoid * **Assuming destiny:** Believing your child will definitely get arthritis because you have it – most children of people with arthritis do not develop the condition. * **Ignoring early signs:** Dismissing joint pain or swelling in children as "growing pains" – consult a professional for new or persistent symptoms. * **Over-restricting activity:** Preventing children from playing sports or being active due to fear of joint damage – tailored physical activity is crucial for joint health. * **Self-diagnosing:** Using internet searches to diagnose your child's symptoms – always seek expert medical opinion. * **Focusing solely on genetics:** Overlooking the important role of healthy lifestyle choices in managing risk – encourage a balanced diet and regular exercise. ## When to Speak to a Clinician If you have concerns about your child's risk of developing arthritis, or if they are showing any new or persistent symptoms, it's always best to have a chat with a doctor. Early diagnosis and intervention can make a significant difference. * Persistent joint pain or stiffness, especially in the morning. * Swelling, warmth, or redness in one or more joints that doesn't go away. * Unexplained limping or difficulty with everyday movements. * Ongoing fatigue that impacts daily activities. * Fever alongside joint symptoms without an obvious cause like an infection. ## Frequently Asked Questions ### Can my child be tested for arthritis genes? While genetic tests exist for some conditions, routine genetic screening for arthritis risk in children isn't usually recommended. The presence of specific genes only indicates a higher susceptibility, not a certainty of developing arthritis, and many other factors are involved. ### What lifestyle changes can help reduce my child's risk? Encouraging a healthy, balanced diet, regular physical activity tailored to their age, maintaining a healthy weight, and avoiding smoking (especially secondhand smoke) can all contribute to overall health and may help reduce the risk of inflammatory conditions. ### If my child develops arthritis, will it be the same type as mine? Not necessarily. While there's an increased risk, it's not guaranteed to be the exact same type of arthritis. Different forms of arthritis have varying genetic predispositions and environmental triggers. ### Practical next steps for Expert Q&A: Will My Children Inherit My Arthritis? article.title: How to Get a Blue Badge for Arthritis in Scotland
article.excerpt: A complete guide to applying for a Blue Badge with arthritis in Scotland — eligibility criteria, the assessment process and what to do if refused.
article.content:
How to get a Blue Badge for arthritis in Scotland — the Blue Badge scheme provides parking concessions that can make an enormous difference to independence and daily life. In Scotland, the scheme is administered by local authorities following national guidelines set by the Scottish Government.

Quick answer: Blue Badge Scotland for arthritis: apply at mygov.scot/blue-badge. Automatic eligibility with PIP/ADP enhanced mobility. Otherwise assessed on walking difficulty. Describe worst typical days, include GP supporting letter, OT report and X-rays if available. Valid UK-wide for 3 years.

Mobility aids and independence — openly licensed via Openverse

Eligibility for Blue Badge in Scotland

You qualify automatically (without assessment) if you receive: the higher rate mobility component of DLA, enhanced rate mobility component of PIP or ADP (Adult Disability Payment — Scotland's equivalent), or War Pensioner's Mobility Supplement.

You may also qualify through assessment if you cannot walk, or have very considerable difficulty walking — including due to severe lower limb arthritis — or have a severe cognitive or psychological impairment. "Very considerable difficulty" is assessed against distance, speed, manner and time taken to walk.

How to Apply in Scotland

  1. Apply online at your local council website or at mygov.scot/blue-badge
  2. Provide: proof of identity, proof of address, a recent photo, details of your condition and how it affects walking
  3. If not automatically eligible, you will be invited to a mobility assessment — in person or by phone
  4. Describe your worst typical walking experience — not an optimistic estimate of what you can achieve with effort

Knee arthritis and mobility — openly licensed via Openverse

Supporting Evidence

A supporting letter from your GP or specialist describing your functional limitations significantly improves success. If you have an OT assessment or mobility report, include this. X-ray reports demonstrating severe joint changes in knees or hips support your application for OA.

If Refused

You can request a review of the decision through your local council's internal process. If this fails, you can escalate to the Scottish Government's Blue Badge Independent Review Service. The Disability Law Service (020 7791 9800) can advise on challenging decisions.

Independence support — openly licensed via Openverse

Short answer: Yes — a Blue Badge issued in Scotland is valid across the UK, including in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. It is also recognised in some European countries.

Short answer: Blue Badges are issued for up to 3 years. Multiple systematic reviews confirm aquatic exercise reduces pain and improves function in hip OA.

Quick answer: Best swimming exercises for hip OA: hip circles, side steps, forward/backward water walking, hip flexion lifts and floating hip abduction. Backstroke is the best stroke for hip OA. Warm water (32-35°C) reduces stiffness. Water reduces joint load by up to 90% compared to land exercise.

Low-impact exercise for hip OA — openly licensed via Openverse

Why Swimming Helps Hip OA

The hip joint is the body's largest weight-bearing joint. In severe OA, even standing transmits painful load through damaged cartilage. Water removes most of this load while still providing resistance for strengthening. Water pressure also reduces swelling and improves proprioception (joint position sense). A 2020 Cochrane review found aquatic exercise produced clinically meaningful improvements in hip OA pain and function compared to no exercise.

Pool Exercises for Hip OA

Hip Circles (Standing in Water)

Stand in chest-deep water, holding pool edge for balance. Draw large slow circles with each hip — 10 clockwise and 10 anti-clockwise per side. Improves hip joint mobility in all planes.

Side Steps

In waist-deep water, step sideways 20 steps in each direction. Water provides lateral resistance without impact. Targets hip abductors — the muscles most important for reducing OA-related limp and hip load.

Forward and Backward Walking

Walk forwards and backwards in chest-deep water for 2–3 minutes. Water resistance provides strengthening without land-based impact. Progress by increasing depth to reduce buoyancy support as strength improves.

Aquatic therapy — openly licensed via Openverse

Hip Flexion Lifts

Stand holding pool edge. Slowly raise one knee to 90 degrees, hold 3 seconds, lower slowly. 12 repetitions each side. Builds hip flexor strength without compressive load.

Floating Hip Abduction

Float on back with noodle under knees. Slowly move legs apart (abduction) and together (adduction) against water resistance. 15 repetitions. Gentle and effective for hip abductor strengthening.

Swimming Strokes Ranked for Hip OA

  • Backstroke: Best — minimal hip rotation, gentle rhythmic movement
  • Front crawl: Good — moderate hip extension and flexion
  • Breaststroke: Use with caution — wide hip rotation can stress medial joint in advanced OA

Question: Can I swim after hip replacement?
Short answer: Usually yes, after approximately 6–12 weeks post-surgery when the wound is fully healed and your surgeon has cleared you. Swimming is often one of the first activities recommended post-hip replacement for its low-impact rehabilitation value.

Question: Is heated pool water better for arthritis?
Short answer: Warm water (32–35°C) is preferred for arthritis exercise — it relaxes muscles, reduces stiffness and is more comfortable for movement. article.title: How to Explain Juvenile Arthritis to School Teachers UK
article.excerpt: A practical guide to explaining juvenile arthritis to teachers — what to cover, how to communicate and what adjustments to request.
article.content:
How to explain juvenile arthritis to school teachers UK — most teachers have never encountered juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) and have no formal training in it. A clear, brief and specific briefing from you as a parent or from the child themselves (for older pupils) dramatically improves the quality of school support your child receives.

Quick answer: When explaining JIA to school teachers: provide a one-page briefing covering what JIA is, what a bad day looks like, which adjustments help (seating, laptop, extra time, flexible PE) and what to do in a flare. Involve the SENCo for formal adjustments. Equality Act 2010 requires schools to make reasonable adjustments.

Child with arthritis school support — openly licensed via Openverse

What Teachers Need to Know

Teachers do not need to become medical experts. They need to understand four things: what JIA is in simple terms, what it looks like on a bad day, what adjustments help and what to do in an emergency.

Suggested Briefing Content (One Page Maximum)

What Is JIA?

"[Child's name] has juvenile idiopathic arthritis — a condition where the immune system causes inflammation in the joints. It is not the same as adult arthritis from old age. It can cause joint pain, stiffness (especially in the morning), fatigue and — during flares — significant limitation in movement. It is unpredictable: some days are fine, other days are much harder. This variability is part of the condition, not inconsistency."

What a Bad Day Looks Like

"On bad days or during a flare, [name] may: move more slowly, struggle to write or type for extended periods, need to sit closer to the exit, appear fatigued even early in the day, or need to take medication at school."

School support for child arthritis — openly licensed via Openverse

Adjustments That Help

  • Seating near the exit to reduce walking distance
  • Permission to use a laptop for extended writing tasks
  • Extra time in assessments (arranged through the SENCo)
  • Flexibility on PE — adapted activities, not exclusion
  • A second set of materials to avoid heavy bag carrying
  • Unrestricted toilet access

In an Emergency

"If [name] appears to have a severely swollen, hot joint alongside fever — contact parents immediately and consider urgent medical attention."

Who Else at School Should Know?

Head of Year or Form Tutor, SENCo (Special Educational Needs Coordinator), PE teacher, and the school nurse if available.

School and medical coordination — openly licensed via Openverse

Q&A

Question: Does the school have a legal obligation to make adjustments?
Short answer: Yes. The Equality Act 2010 requires schools to make reasonable adjustments for children with disabilities. JIA almost certainly qualifies as a disability under the Act.

Question: What if the teacher is dismissive?
Short answer: Escalate to the SENCo or Head of Year in writing. If unresolved, contact the local authority SEND team. article.title: Expert Q&A: How to Evaluate a Clinical Trial Invitation
article.excerpt: Questions to ask before signing the consent form.
article.content:
Quick answer: Before joining a clinical trial, ask about its purpose, the treatments involved, and its duration. Inquire about expectations, potential risks and benefits, and what happens once the trial concludes. Ensure you understand how participation might affect your regular medical care and clarify who to contact with questions. You can withdraw from a trial at any time.

## Overview Questions to ask before signing the consent form. ## What the evidence shows UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Versus Arthritis consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus. ## What this means for you - **Talk to your clinician.** Personalised advice always beats blanket rules. - **Track your symptoms.** Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days. - **Move within comfort.** Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood. - **Watch the warning signs.** New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review. ## Practical next steps 1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: [related guidance](/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis). 2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment. 3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day. ## Editorial standards This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis Editorial Team and reviewed by our Clinical Review Board against UK NICE guidance and peer-reviewed sources. We update content at least annually. ## What the Evidence Says Current evidence from systematic reviews consistently highlights the importance of shared decision-making in healthcare, particularly when considering clinical trials. This means that patients and clinicians work together to make choices about care, taking into account the best available research evidence and the patient's individual values and preferences. Clinical guidelines from professional bodies also stress the ethical imperative of informed consent, ensuring participants fully understand the implications of joining a trial. Randomised controlled trials, the gold standard for testing new interventions, rely on volunteers who are fully aware of what their participation entails. Reviews of trial participation emphasise that clarity of information, presented in an easy-to-understand way, is crucial for people to make a genuine choice. This includes understanding potential benefits, risks, and the commitment involved. ## Common Mistakes to Avoid * **Assuming 'experimental' means 'better':** A new treatment is still unproven, even if it sounds promising. *Always ask about the current standard of care and how the experimental treatment compares.* * **Not asking about costs:** While trial participation itself shouldn't cost you money, travel or time off work might. *Clarify any potential indirect costs before you commit.* * **Feeling pressured to say yes:** You have the right to decline an invitation to a trial without affecting your ongoing care. *Take your time, discuss it with someone you trust, and only agree if you feel comfortable.* * **Not understanding the time commitment involved:** Some trials require frequent visits or lengthy appointments. *Ask for a clear schedule of appointments and procedures.* * **Forgetting you can withdraw:** You can leave a clinical trial at any time, for any reason, even if you've already started. *Remember this right and don't feel trapped.* * **Not clarifying who to contact with questions or problems:** You should have a clear point of contact during the trial. *Ensure you have the name and phone number of the research team member who can help you.* ## When to Speak to a Clinician If you've been invited to a clinical trial and have concerns, or if new symptoms develop during your participation, it's always wise to discuss them with your general practitioner, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist. They can offer an objective perspective and help you weigh your options or address any issues that arise. * You're experiencing new or worsening pain after starting a trial. * You're unsure about the information you've been given about the trial. * You feel uncomfortable or pressured to continue participating. * You're developing side effects that weren't clearly explained. * Your general health changes in a way that might affect your trial participation. ## Frequently Asked Questions ### What kind of questions should I ask before joining a clinical trial? You should ask about the purpose of the trial, what treatments are being studied, how long it will last, what's expected of you, and any potential risks or benefits. It's also helpful to ask about what happens after the trial ends. ### Will participating in a clinical trial affect my regular medical care? Generally, being in a clinical trial should complement your existing care, not replace it. However, some trials might require you to pause or change certain medications or treatments you're currently receiving. Always clarify how the trial might interact with your usual medical routine. ### What happens if a clinical trial drug doesn't work for me, or I experience side effects? The research team will closely monitor you for any changes or side effects. If a treatment isn't working or causes significant problems, they will discuss your options with you, which may include stopping the trial treatment. You always have the right to withdraw from a trial if you wish. ### Practical next steps for Expert Q&A: How to Evaluate a Clinical Trial Invitation If you came here about **Expert Q&A: How to Evaluate a Clinical Trial Invitation**, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete. In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live. ### Reliable UK sources Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence. ### Reliable UK sources Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence. ### Supplements versus meals Food-first is usually safer than stacking capsules. If you do try a supplement, choose a reputable UK brand, check for interactions with your medicines (especially blood thinners), and give any trial a clear stop date so you can judge whether symptoms truly changed. ### Quick questions about Expert Evaluate Clinical Trial **Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician?** No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team. **How long before I judge whether a change helped?** Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner. **What should I track?** Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings. ### Safety and when to get urgent help This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Finding Groups in Scotland

Versus Arthritis Scotland coordinates volunteer-led support groups across the country — in cities, towns and some rural areas. Search versusarthritis.org/get-help/local-support and enter your postcode to find your nearest group. Call their helpline (0800 5200 520) if your search returns no local results — they can connect you to telephone support if no in-person group is nearby.

NHS Social Prescribing in Scotland

NHS Scotland's GPIMHS (GP Integrated Mental Health and Social Prescribing) and community link worker programmes are widely available across Scottish GP practices. Ask your GP or practice nurse to refer you to a community link worker — they can connect you to local arthritis groups, befriending services, leisure activities and practical support.

  • NRAS Scotland: 0800 298 7650 — rheumatoid arthritis specific support
  • Spondylitis Association Scotland: for ankylosing spondylitis support

  • Fibromyalgia Action UK Scotland: 0300 999 3333

article.title: Expert Q&A: Exercising Through a Flare-Up
article.excerpt: When to push and when to rest.
article.content:
Quick answer: During an arthritis flare-up, the article advises adapting rather than stopping exercise: keep gentle, regular, low-impact movement within comfort, track symptoms, and avoid pushing through sharp pain or increasing activity too quickly. It says guidance and reviews support combined medication, movement and lifestyle support, while new swelling, fever, rapid functional loss or severe symptoms need clinician review.

## Overview When to push and when to rest. ## What the evidence shows UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Versus Arthritis consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus. ## What this means for you - **Talk to your clinician.** Personalised advice always beats blanket rules. - **Track your symptoms.** Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days. - **Move within comfort.** Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood. - **Watch the warning signs.** New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review. ## Practical next steps 1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: [related guidance](/arthritis-flare-ups). 2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment. 3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day. ## Editorial standards This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis Editorial Team and reviewed by our Clinical Review Board against UK NICE guidance and peer-reviewed sources. We update content at least annually. ## What the Evidence Says Systematic reviews of physical activity in inflammatory arthritis consistently show that regular, moderate exercise is not only safe but beneficial, even during periods of increased disease activity. These reviews, which pull together findings from many individual randomised trials, indicate that tailored exercise programmes can reduce pain, improve physical function, and enhance quality of life without worsening inflammation. Clinical guidelines from professional bodies universally recommend that people with arthritis remain as active as possible, adapting their exercise routine during flare-ups rather than stopping altogether. The evidence suggests that complete rest for extended periods can actually be detrimental, leading to muscle weakness, joint stiffness, and a poorer long-term outlook. Emerging research, including observational studies, further supports the idea that understanding your body's signals and adjusting activity levels accordingly is key. This 'listen to your body' approach, guided by health professionals, helps maintain conditioning and mental well-being, both crucial for managing long-term conditions. ## Common Mistakes to Avoid * **Pushing through sharp pain:** Pain is a warning sign; ignore it at your peril. *Fix: Reduce intensity or stop the activity immediately.* * **Stopping all movement entirely:** Complete inactivity can cause stiffness and weakness. *Fix: Opt for gentle, non-weight-bearing exercises like stretching or swimming.* * **Increasing activity too quickly after a flare:** This can trigger a relapse. *Fix: Gradually reintroduce activities, increasing duration and intensity slowly over days or weeks.* * **Ignoring new or worsening symptoms:** Changes might indicate a need to adjust treatment. *Fix: Document new symptoms and discuss them with your healthcare provider.* * **Skipping warm-ups and cool-downs:** These prepare your joints and muscles. *Fix: Always include 5-10 minutes of gentle warm-up and cool-down stretches.* ## When to Speak to a Clinician While it's often possible to manage exercise during a flare-up with careful self-monitoring, there are times when it's important to seek advice from your GP, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist. They can help rule out other issues, adjust your medication, or provide a revised exercise plan tailored to your current symptoms. * Sudden, severe, or unexplained pain. * New or rapidly worsening joint swelling that doesn't subside. * Fevers, chills, or a general feeling of being unwell (systemic symptoms). * Significant unexpected weight loss. * Persistent pain or fatigue that doesn't improve with rest or adjusted activity. ## Frequently Asked Questions ### Can exercise make my flare-up worse? When done carefully and gently, exercise during a flare-up is unlikely to make it worse. The key is to listen to your body, reduce intensity, and focus on gentle movement rather than strenuous activity. Avoiding complete immobility can prevent stiffness and muscle loss. ### What types of exercise are best during a flare-up? Low-impact activities like gentle stretching, swimming or hydrotherapy, tai chi, or slow walking are often recommended. These types of exercise help maintain joint mobility and muscle strength without putting undue stress on inflamed joints. ### How do I know if I'm doing too much? Pay attention to increased pain, swelling, or fatigue within an hour or two after exercising, or the next day. If these symptoms are significantly worse, it's a sign you may have pushed too hard and should reduce the intensity or duration next time. ### Practical next steps for Expert Q&A: Exercising Through a Flare-Up If you came here about **Expert Q&A: Exercising Through a Flare-Up**, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete. In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live. ### Making information usable Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone. ### Reliable UK sources Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence. ### Finding people who understand Local arthritis groups, hospital patient panels and moderated online communities can reduce isolation. Ask your rheumatology nurse, library, or council adult social care pages for current lists. Choose spaces that feel practical and kind; leave any that push unproven cures or shame medication use. ### Quick questions about Expert Exercising Through Flare **Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician?** No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team. **How long before I judge whether a change helped?** Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner. **What should I track?** Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings. ### Safety and when to get urgent help This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous. ### Keep learning with us Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis UK — try the [guides hub](/guides), [diet hub](/diet), [exercise hub](/exercises), or [site search](/search) to filter by topic and length. ## What the evidence says 10 Arthritis-Friendly Hobbies UK Patients Love is one of the most discussed challenges in UK arthritis care. Recent reviews — including NICE guidance and Cochrane summaries — point to a clear pattern: small, consistent changes beat heroic one-off efforts. ## Why this matters for social & leisure People living with arthritis report that social & leisure is a daily reality, not a "nice to have". When this area is well-managed, pain scores drop, function improves, and flare frequency falls. When it's ignored, the opposite happens — and the costs compound over months. ## A simple framework you can use this week 1. **Notice** — track one specific factor for three days (e.g. pain after activity, sleep hours, stress level). 2. **Adjust** — change one variable at a time so you can see what's actually working. 3. **Review** — after a week, compare notes. Keep what helps, drop what doesn't. ## What UK clinicians recommend NHS physiotherapists and rheumatology nurses we work with consistently highlight: - **Pacing over pushing** — short, frequent activity beats long, intense sessions. - **Heat for stiffness, cold for swelling** — applied in 15-minute windows. - **Social support** — patients with strong networks report 25% less pain interference. - **Professional guidance early** — don't wait for things to "settle on their own". ## Common myths to ignore - "Rest is always best." Not true — appropriate movement is medicine. - "It's all in your head." Pain is real; psychology helps because the brain processes pain, not because the pain is imaginary. - "Nothing can be done." article.title: How to Get PIP for Fibromyalgia Denied on First Application
article.excerpt: What to do when PIP is denied for fibromyalgia — reapplication strategy, mandatory reconsideration and tribunal success tips.
article.content:
How to get PIP for fibromyalgia denied on first application — first-time refusal for fibromyalgia is common, but overturn rates on appeal and reapplication are high. This guide explains your options clearly.

Quick answer: If PIP is denied for fibromyalgia: request mandatory reconsideration in writing within 1 month, including GP letter on functional limitations and OT assessment if available. If MR fails, appeal to SSCS Tribunal (free, 60-70% success rate with evidence). Citizens Advice (0800 144 8848) provides free representation.

Benefits support — openly licensed via Openverse

Why Fibromyalgia Claims Are Often Refused

Fibromyalgia is an invisible condition — there is no blood test or imaging that confirms it, assessors cannot see the pain, and the variable nature of the condition means some people appear "well" at assessment. DWP assessors frequently underestimate functional impact from fibromyalgia. This is why challenge rates are high — and why the evidence you provide matters enormously.

Option 1: Mandatory Reconsideration

If refused, you have 1 month to request a Mandatory Reconsideration (MR) in writing. Do not call — write a detailed letter. Address each activity the DWP scored you lower on and explain specifically why their assessment was wrong. Include new evidence: GP letter emphasising functional limitations (not just diagnosis), medication list with side effects, and — most powerfully — an OT or physiotherapy functional assessment.

Functional impact documentation — openly licensed via Openverse

Option 2: Tribunal Appeal

If the MR is refused, appeal to the SSCS Tribunal (free). Tribunal success rates for fibromyalgia with medical evidence are 60–70%. Key for tribunal success:

  • Attend in person if you can — attendance significantly improves success rates
  • Bring a supporter or representative (Citizens Advice can often provide representation)
  • Have a GP or specialist letter specifically addressing the tribunal's schedule of descriptors
  • Describe your very worst days in detail

Option 3: New Application

If your condition has worsened since your last application, or significant time has passed, a new application may be more appropriate than continuing to appeal an old decision. A new application is assessed on current circumstances.

Support with appeals — openly licensed via Openverse

Q&A

Question: How do I get Citizens Advice help with my PIP appeal?
Short answer: Call 0800 144 8848 or visit citizensadvice.org.uk to find your nearest office and book an appointment. Many offices have specialist benefits advisers who handle PIP appeals regularly.

Question: Will appealing affect my other benefits?
Short answer: No. Appealing PIP does not affect other means-tested benefits.
