article.title: Best Exercises for Rheumatoid Arthritis in Hands and Wrists
article.excerpt: A clinically reviewed programme of the best exercises for RA affecting hands and wrists — improving grip, reducing stiffness and maintaining function.
article.content:
Best exercises for rheumatoid arthritis in hands and wrists — RA most commonly begins in the small joints of the hands and wrists. Regular hand and wrist exercises are one of the most important self-management strategies for maintaining grip strength, reducing stiffness and preserving function.

Quick answer: Best exercises for RA hands and wrists: tendon gliding, wrist flexion/extension, radial/ulnar deviation, soft foam grip squeezes, finger spreading. Do after morning stiffness eases, soak hands in warm water first. During flares: range-of-motion only, no resistance. Expect reduced stiffness in 2-3 weeks.

Arthritic hands — openly licensed via Openverse

Why Hand Exercises Are Essential in RA

RA causes synovitis (inflammation of the joint lining) in the hand and wrist joints, leading to pain, swelling and — if untreated — joint damage and deformity. Exercise does not cure or stop the inflammatory process, but it maintains the strength and range of motion that functional deformity threatens to reduce. NICE guidance recommends hand exercises as part of standard RA management.

The Core Hand and Wrist Programme

Tendon Gliding Exercises

Start with hand flat (extension), make a hook (straight fingers bent at middle joints), then full fist, then straight fist (fingers bent, thumb alongside). Hold each position 3 seconds. 10 repetitions each hand. These maintain full tendon movement through the hand.

Wrist Flexion and Extension

Rest forearm on a table, hand extending over the edge. Slowly bend wrist downward (flexion) and upward (extension) through full range. 10 repetitions each direction, both wrists.

Radial and Ulnar Deviation

Forearm flat, palm down. Move hand toward thumb side (radial deviation), then little finger side (ulnar deviation). 10 repetitions. Important for maintaining wrist side-to-side movement often lost early in RA wrist disease.

Rheumatoid arthritis hand changes — openly licensed via Openverse

Pinch and Grip Strengthening

Squeeze a soft foam ball or rolled-up towel 10 times each hand. Pinch a clothes peg open using thumb and each finger in turn. Do not use hard grip strengtheners during active inflammation — the resistance is too high.

Finger Spreading

Place hand flat on table. Spread fingers as wide as possible, hold 3 seconds, bring together. 10 repetitions. Maintains MCP joint mobility.

Timing and Flare Management

Perform exercises after morning stiffness has eased — typically 1–2 hours after waking or after medication has taken effect. Warm water soaking (5 minutes in warm water) before exercises significantly reduces stiffness. During a flare: gentle range-of-motion only, no resistance work. Resume strengthening 2–3 days after swelling reduces.

Question: Should I wear splints alongside exercises?
Short answer: Resting splints worn at night reduce joint loading and morning stiffness in RA. Working splints (softer, worn during activity) can support wrists during tasks. An occupational therapist can advise on the right type for your specific pattern of involvement.

Question: When will I notice improvement?
Short answer: Reduced morning stiffness is typically noticed within 2–3 weeks of consistent daily practice. Grip strength improvements take 6–8 weeks. ### Practical next steps for Best Exercises for Rheumatoid Arthritis in Hands and Wrists If you came here about **Best Exercises for Rheumatoid Arthritis in Hands and Wrists**, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. article.title: Foods to Avoid With Arthritis: A Complete UK Guide
article.excerpt: Discover which foods trigger inflammation and joint pain — and what to eat instead.
article.content:
Quick answer: For arthritis, the guide advises limiting ultra-processed foods, sugary drinks, refined carbohydrates, omega-6-rich vegetable oils and fried foods, alcohol, especially beer for gout, high-salt processed foods and sometimes full-fat dairy. It says these can worsen inflammation, uric acid, swelling and joint pain, while wholegrains, oily fish, vegetables, olive oil, nuts and seeds are suggested swaps.

If you live with arthritis in the UK, you already know that pain and stiffness can fluctuate from one day to the next. While there is no single diet that cures arthritis, mounting research confirms that certain foods consistently worsen inflammation — the very process driving joint damage and pain. Understanding which foods to avoid with arthritis is one of the most practical, cost-free steps you can take alongside your prescribed treatment. This guide covers the key dietary culprits identified in clinical research, explains why they affect your joints, and offers simple swaps you can make today. Whether you have osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, or gout, the principles largely overlap. ## Why Does Diet Affect Arthritis? Arthritis is broadly an inflammatory condition. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) involves an overactive immune system attacking joint tissue; osteoarthritis (OA) involves cartilage breakdown accompanied by low-grade inflammation. Either way, what you eat directly influences your body's inflammatory pathways. Certain foods raise levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, TNF-alpha, and CRP — markers commonly measured in blood tests for arthritis. Others flood the bloodstream with advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) that stiffen joint tissue. A 2023 review published in *Nutrients* found that patients who reduced processed food consumption reported a statistically significant reduction in pain scores within 12 weeks. ## 1. Ultra-Processed Foods and Fast Food Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) — including ready meals, crisps, packaged biscuits, processed meats such as sausages and deli slices, and fast-food items — are the biggest dietary threat for people with arthritis. They are dense in trans fats, refined carbohydrates, artificial additives, and preservatives, all of which promote systemic inflammation. A UK Biobank study found that higher UPF consumption was independently associated with increased odds of developing inflammatory arthritis. If a food has more than five ingredients on the label and many of them are unrecognisable chemical names, it almost certainly qualifies as ultra-processed. **Quick swaps** - Replace crisps with a small handful of unsalted walnuts or pumpkin seeds. - Swap processed sausages for grilled chicken thighs or oily fish. - Choose homemade soups over tinned varieties loaded with sodium and additives. ## 2. Sugar and High-Fructose Foods Sugar is a powerful inflammation trigger. Excess sugar in the diet raises blood glucose, which in turn stimulates the release of inflammatory cytokines. It also encourages weight gain — and every extra kilogram places roughly four kilograms of additional stress on each knee joint. High-fructose corn syrup, commonly found in fizzy drinks, energy drinks, flavoured yogurts, and many breakfast cereals, is particularly harmful. Fructose is metabolised by the liver and, in excess, converts to uric acid — a direct cause of gout flares. People with gout should be especially vigilant about fruit juices, which can deliver a large fructose hit without the fibre buffer of whole fruit. ## 3. Refined Carbohydrates White bread, white rice, pasta made from refined flour, pastries, and most commercially produced cakes and muffins spike blood sugar rapidly, triggering an inflammatory cascade. They lack the fibre and nutrients of their wholegrain equivalents and offer little benefit to joint health. The glycaemic index (GI) is a useful tool: foods with a GI above 70 — such as white baguette, cornflakes, or instant mashed potato — cause the fastest blood sugar spikes. Swapping these for low-GI alternatives (oats, wholegrain rye bread, sweet potato, brown basmati rice) is one of the most evidence-based dietary changes for reducing arthritis-related inflammation. ## 4. Omega-6 Fatty Acids and Vegetable Oils Not all fats are equal. The typical British diet contains far too many omega-6 fatty acids relative to anti-inflammatory omega-3s. Omega-6 fats, found abundantly in sunflower oil, corn oil, and soya oil — oils used heavily in restaurant cooking and packaged snacks — are precursors to pro-inflammatory eicosanoids. Ideally the omega-6 to omega-3 ratio in the diet should be 4:1 or lower. Many people in the UK currently consume a ratio closer to 15:1 or even 20:1. Reducing fried foods, limiting vegetable oil use at home, and increasing oily fish intake (salmon, mackerel, sardines, herring) is the most practical way to rebalance this ratio. ## 5. Alcohol Alcohol interacts with arthritis in multiple ways. It is directly pro-inflammatory, interfering with the gut microbiome and increasing intestinal permeability — sometimes called 'leaky gut' — which allows bacterial toxins to enter the bloodstream and stimulate immune activation. Beer is particularly problematic for people with gout because it contains both alcohol and purines (compounds that metabolise to uric acid). Even moderate beer consumption can double the risk of a gout attack. Spirits and wine are somewhat lower in purines but still increase uric acid production. If you have gout, the safest approach is to significantly limit or eliminate alcohol, especially beer and stout. ## 6. Dairy Products (For Some People) The evidence on dairy is more nuanced. Full-fat dairy — butter, cream, full-fat cheese, and whole milk — contains saturated fats that can promote inflammation in some individuals, particularly those with RA. However, low-fat dairy such as skimmed milk and low-fat yogurt may actually be protective against gout due to a mechanism that promotes uric acid excretion. If you notice that dairy products worsen your symptoms, consider an elimination trial under the guidance of a registered dietitian. Some people find that switching to plant-based alternatives reduces flare frequency, though evidence for this remains anecdotal for most arthritis types. ## 7. Salt and High-Sodium Foods Excess sodium intake drives fluid retention and can worsen joint swelling. It also appears to activate Th17 immune cells — the same cells implicated in autoimmune forms of arthritis like RA and psoriatic arthritis. Research from Yale University demonstrated that a high-salt diet significantly worsened autoimmune disease in animal models. Processed and takeaway foods are the biggest sources of hidden sodium in the UK diet. UK guidelines recommend no more than 6g of salt per day for adults; many takeaway meals contain this in a single serving. Reading food labels and cooking from scratch are the most effective strategies. ## Quick Answer People with arthritis should avoid ultra-processed foods, sugary drinks, refined carbohydrates, foods high in omega-6 fats (like sunflower-oil-fried foods), alcohol (especially beer if you have gout), and high-sodium processed foods. These foods increase inflammation, raise uric acid levels, and worsen joint pain. ## What Should You Eat Instead? An anti-inflammatory diet rich in oily fish, colourful vegetables, legumes, wholegrains, olive oil, nuts, and seeds is strongly associated with reduced arthritis symptoms. The Mediterranean diet, in particular, has robust clinical evidence behind it for RA and OA. Aim to fill half your plate with vegetables at every meal, choose oily fish at least twice a week, and use extra-virgin olive oil as your primary cooking fat. ## Practical Steps Starting Today You do not need to overhaul your entire diet at once. Start with these three changes: 1. Cut out fizzy drinks and fruit juice — replace with water, herbal teas, or green tea. 2. Switch to wholegrain bread and pasta instead of white versions. 3. Add one portion of oily fish per week if you do not already eat it. Track your symptoms in a food and pain diary over four to six weeks. Many people with arthritis notice a meaningful difference within this timeframe when they reduce the foods listed in this article. ## Conclusion Managing arthritis is a lifelong journey, and diet is one of the few areas where you have real, daily control. While no food change replaces your prescribed medication or physiotherapy, reducing your intake of ultra-processed foods, sugar, refined carbs, excess omega-6 fats, alcohol, and salt can meaningfully reduce inflammation and improve your quality of life. For personalised advice, ask your GP for a referral to a registered dietitian who specialises in musculoskeletal conditions.

article.title: Nutrition Strategies to Reduce Frailty Risk
article.excerpt: Good nutrition is one of the most powerful, modifiable tools for preventing and managing frailty. Here's what to prioritise.
article.content:
Quick answer: Frailty is linked to unintentional weight loss and inadequate nutrient intake. Optimising nutrition — particularly protein intake of 1.0–1.2 grams per kilogram of body weight daily, plus Vitamin D, calcium, B vitamins and adequate fluid — helps manage it. Addressing barriers like reduced appetite or dental issues, and seeking guidance from a registered dietitian, improves outcomes.

Nutrition plays a central role in both preventing and managing frailty. Unintentional weight loss and inadequate nutrient intake are among the core features used to identify frailty clinically, and malnutrition can both contribute to and worsen the condition. The encouraging news is that nutrition is one of the most modifiable risk factors available, meaning meaningful change is achievable at almost any stage. A registered dietitian can provide personalised guidance, but understanding key nutritional principles can help you make better choices. ## Why Nutrition Matters So Much for Frailty As we age, nutritional needs actually increase in some ways while appetite and food intake may decrease. This is a dangerous mismatch. The body needs more protein to maintain muscle, more calcium and vitamin D for bones, adequate fibre and fluid for digestive health, yet many older adults consume fewer calories and less of essential nutrients. Poor nutrition weakens muscle, slows bone healing, impairs immune function, and delays recovery from illness or injury. It's directly involved in the mechanisms that create frailty. Conversely, optimising nutrition can slow frailty's progression and even improve function in people already frail. ## Protein: The Building Block of Muscle As we age, the body becomes somewhat less efficient at using dietary protein to build and maintain muscle, a phenomenon sometimes called "anabolic resistance." This means older adults often need more protein, not less, compared to younger adults, to maintain the same muscle mass. Current recommendations suggest older adults need approximately 1.0-1.2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight daily. For a 70-kilogram person, that's 70-84 grams daily — roughly 25-30 grams per meal spread across three meals, plus a snack. Good sources include lean meat, fish, eggs, dairy, legumes, and tofu. The key is including protein at each meal. Some people find concentrated sources like Greek yoghurt, cottage cheese, or a glass of milk at breakfast helpful ways to increase intake without dramatically changing portions. ## Key Vitamins and Minerals Vitamin D supports both bone and muscle health, and deficiency is common among older adults, particularly those with limited sun exposure. The recommended dietary allowance for adults over 70 is 800 IU daily, but many people need supplementation to achieve adequate levels. Calcium works alongside vitamin D to protect bone density. Dairy products, fortified plant-based milks, and leafy greens are good sources, though meeting the 1,000-1,200 mg daily recommendation for older adults often requires deliberate effort. B vitamins support energy metabolism and nerve function. A deficiency in vitamin B12, which is common in older adults and particularly in people taking certain medications for diabetes or acid reflux, can contribute to weakness and cognitive problems. Adequate fibre and fluid intake support digestive health, which can otherwise affect appetite and nutrient absorption. Older adults sometimes don't drink enough fluid, which can lead to dehydration affecting energy and cognition. Iron, zinc, and magnesium also play important roles in muscle function and overall health, and deficiencies are more common in older adults than many realise. ## Addressing Common Barriers to Eating Well Several factors can make it harder for older adults to eat enough, including reduced appetite, difficulty chewing or swallowing, limited mobility for shopping and cooking, medication side effects that affect appetite or taste, and social isolation, which can reduce motivation to prepare and enjoy meals. Dental problems are surprisingly common and often overlooked. Someone with poorly fitting dentures or missing teeth may avoid foods they should be eating. A dentist can help address these issues. Medications can affect appetite, taste, or nutrient absorption. A pharmacist can sometimes suggest timing adjustments or alternative medications with fewer effects on nutrition. Limited mobility for shopping and cooking can be addressed through meal delivery services, online shopping with home delivery, or asking family and friends for support. Some communities offer meal delivery programmes for older adults. Social isolation is both a cause and consequence of poor nutrition. Eating with others — even occasionally — can improve both nutrition and wellbeing. Some communities offer group meal programmes. ## Practical Tips for Better Nutrition Eating smaller, more frequent, nutrient-dense meals can help when appetite is limited. Rather than three large meals, having five or six smaller ones spreads nutrition throughout the day and may feel less overwhelming. Adding protein or calorie-dense additions like nut butter, cheese, seeds, or olive oil to meals can boost intake without requiring larger portions. A piece of toast with almond butter provides more nutrition than plain toast. Smoothies made with milk or yoghurt, fruit, and protein powder can be an easy way to increase protein and calorie intake if swallowing is difficult. Staying hydrated supports overall function and appetite. Many older adults don't drink enough water. Setting reminders or keeping a water bottle visible can help. For those at higher risk of malnutrition, a registered dietitian can provide a personalised nutrition plan tailored to specific health conditions and preferences. In the UK, a referral to dietetics services can sometimes be obtained through your GP. ## Bringing It Together Combined with regular physical activity, particularly resistance exercise, good nutrition forms one of the two pillars of frailty prevention and management. Small, consistent improvements in diet can have a meaningful impact on strength, energy, and independence over time. **This article is for general information only and is not a substitute for professional medical advice. Always consult with your healthcare provider or a registered dietitian before making significant changes to your diet, particularly if you have medical conditions or take medications that affect nutrition.** ### Practical next steps for Nutrition Strategies to Reduce Frailty Risk If you came here about **Nutrition Strategies to Reduce Frailty Risk**, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete. In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live. ### Everyday eating patterns No single food cures arthritis. Patterns rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses, wholegrains and oily fish are the ones most often discussed in UK dietetic advice for inflammatory conditions. Keep changes realistic: swap one ultra-processed snack for fruit and nuts, or cook with olive oil more often than seed oils marketed as miracle cures. ### Supplements versus meals Food-first is usually safer than stacking capsules. If you do try a supplement, choose a reputable UK brand, check for interactions with your medicines (especially blood thinners), and give any trial a clear stop date so you can judge whether symptoms truly changed. ### Using evidence carefully Marketing claims for joint supplements often outrun the research. Look for products that state dose clearly, avoid miracle language, and fit alongside — never instead of — prescribed treatment. Stop and seek advice if you notice bruising, stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or new rashes. ### Quick questions about Nutrition Strategies Reduce Frailty **Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician?** No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team. **How long before I judge whether a change helped?** Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner. **What should I track?** Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings. ### Safety and when to get urgent help This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous. ### Keep learning with us Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis UK — try the [guides hub](/guides), [diet hub](/diet), [exercise hub](/exercises), or [site search](/search) to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the [Benefits & PIP hub](/benefits-pip).

article.title: Inflammatory Arthritis: Types, Causes and Treatment
article.excerpt: Inflammatory arthritis covers conditions like rheumatoid, psoriatic and reactive arthritis, where the immune system — not wear and tear — drives joint damage. Here is what makes it different and how it is treated.
article.content:
Quick answer: Inflammatory arthritis is an umbrella term for immune-driven joint conditions (rheumatoid, psoriatic, reactive arthritis and more), distinct from the mechanical wear of osteoarthritis. It typically causes morning stiffness over 30 minutes, joint swelling and fatigue, and is treated with immune-modulating medication such as DMARDs or biologics alongside exercise and lifestyle measures.

## What Is Inflammatory Arthritis? Inflammatory arthritis is an umbrella term for a group of conditions where the immune system itself causes joint pain, swelling and stiffness — rather than joints simply wearing down over time. This is the key difference from osteoarthritis, the "wear and tear" type most people picture when they hear the word arthritis. In inflammatory arthritis, the immune system mistakenly attacks the lining of the joints (or, in some cases, entheses — the points where tendons attach to bone), triggering ongoing inflammation that can damage cartilage and bone if it isn't treated. Conditions that fall under this umbrella include rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, and polymyalgia rheumatica. Each has its own pattern and triggers, but they share a common thread: the pain and stiffness come from active inflammation, not mechanical damage, and they generally respond to different treatments than osteoarthritis does. ## How It Differs From Osteoarthritis The distinction matters because it changes what actually helps. - **Osteoarthritis** tends to affect joints that have taken the most physical load over the years — knees, hips, hands — and symptoms typically get worse with activity and better with rest. Treatment focuses on exercise, weight management, and pain relief. - **Inflammatory arthritis** often causes morning stiffness lasting longer than 30 minutes to an hour, can affect smaller joints symmetrically (both hands, both wrists), and may come with fatigue, low-grade fever, or symptoms elsewhere in the body (skin, eyes, gut). Because the root cause is an overactive immune response, treatment usually involves medications that calm the immune system down — not just manage the symptoms. Getting the right diagnosis early matters a great deal with inflammatory types, because unlike osteoarthritis, untreated inflammation can cause irreversible joint damage within months, not years. ## Common Symptoms to Watch For - Joint stiffness that is worse first thing in the morning and takes a long time to ease - Swelling, warmth or redness over a joint, not just pain - Symptoms affecting several joints at once, sometimes symmetrically - Fatigue that feels disproportionate to how active you've been - In some types: skin changes (psoriasis-like patches), eye redness or irritation, or digestive symptoms - Symptoms that don't settle with rest the way mechanical joint pain usually does No single symptom confirms inflammatory arthritis on its own — a GP will usually combine your symptom pattern with blood tests (such as CRP, ESR, rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP antibodies) and sometimes imaging to work out which type, if any, is involved. ## How Inflammatory Arthritis Is Diagnosed Diagnosis typically starts with a GP, who will ask about your symptom pattern — which joints, how long stiffness lasts, whether it's improved or worsened by movement — and examine the affected joints for swelling or warmth. Blood tests looking for markers of inflammation and specific antibodies help narrow down the type, though a normal blood test doesn't fully rule out inflammatory arthritis, since some people have "seronegative" disease. If inflammatory arthritis is suspected, the next step is usually a referral to a rheumatologist — a specialist in this exact area — ideally within weeks rather than months, since early treatment with disease-modifying drugs has consistently been shown to give better long-term joint outcomes than delayed treatment. ## Treatment Approaches Because inflammatory arthritis is driven by the immune system, treatment generally centres on calming that immune response, alongside the same lifestyle measures that help any type of arthritis: - **DMARDs (disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs)**, such as methotrexate, are often the first line of treatment for conditions like rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis. They work by dampening the underlying immune activity, not just masking pain. - **Biologic therapies** target specific parts of the immune system more precisely and are typically considered when standard DMARDs aren't enough on their own. - **Short-term steroids** (oral or injected) can bring rapid relief during a flare while longer-term treatments take effect. - **NSAIDs and pain relief** help manage symptoms day to day but don't address the underlying inflammation on their own. - **Physiotherapy and gentle, regular exercise** remain important across all types of arthritis — they help maintain joint function and muscle support even while medication addresses the inflammation itself. Treatment plans are highly individual and depend on which specific condition is involved, how active the disease is, and how you respond to different medications — this is genuinely a case where working closely with a rheumatology team makes a real difference. ## Living With Inflammatory Arthritis Day to Day A diagnosis of inflammatory arthritis is often a lifelong one, but for most people, effective treatment means long periods of low disease activity or remission, not constant flares. Practical things that help day to day include: - Pacing activity across the day rather than pushing through until you crash, especially when fatigue is part of your picture - Keeping a simple symptom diary so you and your rheumatology team can spot patterns and adjust treatment before a flare gets out of hand - Staying as physically active as your joints allow — inactivity tends to make stiffness worse, not better - Building a support network, whether that's family, a local support group, or an online community of people managing the same condition - Being upfront with your employer where possible about flexibility needs, since fatigue and flare-ups don't always follow a predictable schedule ## When to Seek Urgent Advice Most inflammatory arthritis symptoms build gradually and can be discussed at a routine GP appointment, but a few situations warrant faster attention: - A single joint that becomes hot, red, swollen and severely painful very suddenly — this can occasionally indicate a joint infection (septic arthritis), which needs same-day assessment rather than a routine appointment - New eye redness or pain alongside joint symptoms, particularly with conditions like ankylosing spondylitis or reactive arthritis, which can involve eye inflammation (uveitis) needing prompt treatment - Signs of a significant flare while on immune-suppressing medication, such as a high fever, since these medications can affect the body's ability to fight infection Knowing these warning signs helps you judge when "wait and see" is reasonable and when it isn't — most day-to-day symptom changes fall into the former category, but it's worth knowing the exceptions. ## The Role of a Multidisciplinary Team Managing inflammatory arthritis well typically involves more than just a rheumatologist. Physiotherapists help maintain joint function and design safe exercise programmes around active disease. Occupational therapists can advise on joint-protection techniques and practical aids for daily tasks during flares. Podiatrists are often involved when arthritis affects the feet, which is common in rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis. Some people also benefit from dietitian input, since maintaining a healthy weight reduces load on affected joints, and specialist nurses often act as the first point of contact between routine rheumatology appointments — genuinely useful for questions that come up between visits rather than waiting months for the next one. ## Frequently Asked Questions **Is inflammatory arthritis the same as rheumatoid arthritis?** No — rheumatoid arthritis is one specific type of inflammatory arthritis. The umbrella term also covers psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica and others, each with different patterns and triggers. **Can inflammatory arthritis be cured?** Most forms can't be cured outright, but modern treatment — particularly when started early — can bring disease activity under control to the point where many people experience long stretches with few or no symptoms. **Does inflammatory arthritis always get worse over time?** Not necessarily. Left untreated, it often does progress and can cause lasting joint damage. With appropriate treatment, though, many people's disease activity stabilises or improves rather than steadily worsening. **Is inflammatory arthritis hereditary?** Some types have a genetic component that increases risk, but genetics alone don't determine whether someone develops the condition — it's generally considered a combination of genetic susceptibility and environmental triggers. ## Key Takeaways - Inflammatory arthritis is an umbrella term for immune-driven joint conditions, distinct from the mechanical wear-and-tear of osteoarthritis. - Morning stiffness lasting over 30 minutes, joint swelling, and disproportionate fatigue are common red flags worth discussing with a GP. - Early diagnosis and treatment matter enormously, since untreated inflammation can cause permanent joint damage. - Treatment usually combines immune-modulating medication with the same exercise and lifestyle measures that help any type of arthritis. - A diagnosis doesn't mean constant symptoms — effective treatment can bring long periods of stability for most people. *This article provides general information and is not a substitute for personalised medical advice. If you're experiencing symptoms of inflammatory arthritis, speak to your GP about a referral to a rheumatologist.*

article.title: JAK Inhibitors: The Next Wave of RA Treatment
article.excerpt: Tofacitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib explained for patients.
article.content:
Quick answer: JAK inhibitors reduce rheumatoid arthritis symptoms like pain, swelling, and stiffness by blocking specific immune system pathways that cause inflammation. They are an option if other treatments haven't worked and can significantly improve quality of life. However, they come with potential side effects, such as infections, and may not be suitable for everyone. Your doctor will assess risks and benefits.

## Overview Tofacitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib explained for patients. ## What the evidence shows UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Versus Arthritis consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus. ## What this means for you - **Talk to your clinician.** Personalised advice always beats blanket rules. - **Track your symptoms.** Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days. - **Move within comfort.** Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood. - **Watch the warning signs.** New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review. ## Practical next steps 1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: [related guidance](/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis). 2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment. 3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day. ## Editorial standards This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis Editorial Team and reviewed by our Clinical Review Board against UK NICE guidance and peer-reviewed sources. We update content at least annually. ## What the Evidence Says Randomised trials have shown that JAK inhibitors (Janus kinase inhibitors) can be very effective in reducing the symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis, such as pain, swelling, and stiffness. These medications work by blocking specific pathways in the immune system that contribute to inflammation. For many people, this can lead to significant improvements in their quality of life. Systematic reviews, which combine the results of multiple studies, confirm these benefits. They also highlight that while these treatments can be powerful, they come with potential side effects that need careful consideration. Clinical guidelines from professional bodies recommend JAK inhibitors for people whose arthritis hasn't responded well to other types of medication, often after trying conventional disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) or biologic therapies. Overall, the picture from the evidence is that JAK inhibitors are an important addition to the treatment options for rheumatoid arthritis, offering a new pathway to manage the condition for those who need it. The focus is always on balancing the benefits of symptom control with managing any potential risks, tailored to each individual's health. ## Common Mistakes to Avoid * **Stopping medication abruptly:** This can lead to your symptoms returning or worsening. Always discuss changes with your doctor first. * **Ignoring side effects:** Even mild side effects should be mentioned to your care team. They can help adjust your treatment or offer solutions. * **Comparing your progress to others:** Everyone's journey with rheumatoid arthritis is unique. Focus on your own improvements and challenges. * **Not asking questions:** If something isn't clear, ask your doctor or nurse. Understanding your treatment helps you manage it better. * **Neglecting regular exercise:** Staying active, even gently, helps maintain joint flexibility and muscle strength. Find what works for you. ## When to Speak to a Clinician While managing rheumatoid arthritis is a long-term journey, there are times when you should seek prompt advice from your doctor, physiotherapist, or rheumatology team. Don't wait for your next routine appointment if you experience any of the following: * Sudden, severe pain or swelling in a joint. * New or worsening fever, especially if accompanied by chills. * Signs of infection, such as redness, warmth, or pus around a joint, or a general feeling of being unwell. * Any new, unexplained symptoms that concern you, particularly if they appear shortly after starting a new medication. * Rapid loss of function or inability to move a joint that was previously manageable. ## Frequently Asked Questions ### What are JAK inhibitors and how do they work? JAK inhibitors are a type of medication that targets specific pathways within your immune system. They block the activity of enzymes called Janus kinases, which play a key role in the inflammatory process linked to rheumatoid arthritis. By doing this, they help to reduce inflammation, pain, and joint damage. ### Are JAK inhibitors suitable for everyone with rheumatoid arthritis? No, they are not suitable for everyone. They are typically considered when other treatments, like conventional DMARDs or biologic therapies, haven't worked well enough for you. Your doctor will assess your overall health, other medical conditions, and potential risks to decide if a JAK inhibitor is a safe and appropriate option for you. ### What are the possible side effects of JAK inhibitors? Like all medications, JAK inhibitors can have side effects. Common ones can include infections (like colds or shingles), headaches, and digestive upset. More serious but less common side effects can include an increased risk of certain serious infections or blood clots. Your doctor will discuss these risks with you before starting treatment and monitor you closely. ### Practical next steps for JAK Inhibitors: The Next Wave of RA Treatment If you came here about **JAK Inhibitors: The Next Wave of RA Treatment**, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete. In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live. ### Preparing for appointments Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book. ### Working with NHS pathways Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates. ### Pacing on good and bad days On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether. ### Quick questions about Inhibitors Next Wave Treatment **Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician?** No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team. **How long before I judge whether a change helped?** Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner. **What should I track?** Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings. ### Safety and when to get urgent help This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous. ### Keep learning with us Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis UK — try the [guides hub](/guides), [diet hub](/diet), [exercise hub](/exercises), or [site search](/search) to filter by topic and length. /blog/anti-inflammatory-herbs-spices-art.answer: Several herbs and spices available in UK shops have genuine anti-inflammatory evidence for arthritis, including turmeric (curcumin), ginger, garlic, cinnamon, rosemary and boswellia. article.title: Anti-Inflammatory Herbs and Spices for Arthritis: A Complete Guide
article.excerpt: Evidence-based guide to anti-inflammatory herbs and spices for arthritis. Learn about ginger, cinnamon, garlic, rosemary and other natural remedies available in the UK.
article.content:
For centuries, herbs and spices have been used to treat pain and inflammation. Modern science is now validating many of these traditional remedies, identifying the specific compounds responsible for their anti-inflammatory effects and testing them in clinical trials. While no herb or spice can replace medical treatment for arthritis, several have genuine evidence supporting their use as complementary approaches. This guide examines the most promising options available in UK shops and supermarkets.

Quick answer: Several herbs and spices available in UK shops have genuine anti-inflammatory evidence for arthritis, including turmeric (curcumin), ginger, garlic, cinnamon, rosemary and boswellia. None replace medical treatment, but the strongest data are for curcumin at around 1,000 mg/day with an absorption aid, and ginger extract at 500–1,000 mg/day. Use consistently for 4–12 weeks before judging effect.

Ginger (Zingiber officinale)

The Evidence

Ginger is one of the most extensively studied anti-inflammatory spices for arthritis. Its active compounds — gingerols, shogaols and paradols — inhibit the same inflammatory pathways (COX-2, LOX, NF-κB) targeted by conventional anti-inflammatory medications. A meta-analysis of five randomised controlled trials found that ginger significantly reduced pain and disability in osteoarthritis, with effects comparable to ibuprofen in some studies. The evidence is strongest for knee osteoarthritis.

How to Use

  • Fresh ginger — Grate 1–2 cm into stir-fries, soups, smoothies or hot water for ginger tea
  • Ground ginger — ½–1 teaspoon daily added to cooking, porridge or warm drinks
  • Supplements — 500–1,000 mg daily of ginger extract (available from Holland & Barrett, Boots)
  • Ginger tea — Steep fresh sliced ginger in boiling water for 10 minutes. Add honey and lemon

Safety

Generally very safe. May cause mild heartburn in some people. Can interact with blood-thinning medications (warfarin) — check with your GP. Not recommended in doses exceeding 4g daily.

Cinnamon (Cinnamomum)

The Evidence

Cinnamon contains cinnamaldehyde and proanthocyanidins, which have demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects in laboratory studies. A systematic review found cinnamon supplementation reduced inflammatory markers (CRP) in people with metabolic conditions. Limited but promising research specifically in arthritis suggests potential benefits for reducing joint inflammation and oxidative stress.

How to Use

  • Sprinkle on porridge, yoghurt, smoothies or baked fruit
  • Add to warm milk or coffee (golden milk with turmeric and cinnamon is popular)
  • Use Ceylon cinnamon ("true cinnamon") rather than cassia cinnamon, as cassia contains higher levels of coumarin which can affect the liver in large amounts
  • 1–3g daily is commonly used

Garlic (Allium sativum)

The Evidence

Garlic contains diallyl disulphide (DADS), a compound that limits cartilage-damaging enzymes in laboratory studies. A large epidemiological study published in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders found that women who consumed more garlic had significantly lower rates of hip osteoarthritis. While clinical trial evidence specifically for arthritis pain is limited, garlic's anti-inflammatory properties are well documented.

How to Use

  • Use 1–2 fresh cloves daily in cooking — crush or chop and let stand for 10 minutes before cooking to maximise allicin production
  • Raw garlic is most potent but harder to tolerate — roasted garlic is milder and still beneficial
  • Aged garlic extract supplements are available for those who dislike the taste

Rosemary (Rosmarinus officinalis)

The Evidence

Rosemary contains rosmarinic acid and carnosic acid, both potent antioxidants with anti-inflammatory properties. Laboratory studies show these compounds inhibit COX-2 and reduce inflammatory cytokines. While clinical trial evidence in arthritis is still emerging, the anti-inflammatory mechanisms are well characterised.

How to Use

  • Add fresh or dried rosemary liberally to roasted vegetables, meats and soups
  • Make rosemary tea by steeping a sprig in hot water for 5–10 minutes
  • Rosemary oil can be used topically (diluted in a carrier oil) for joint massage

Green Tea (Camellia sinensis)

The Evidence

Green tea contains epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), a powerful anti-inflammatory polyphenol. Research published in Arthritis Research & Therapy found EGCG reduced inflammation and cartilage destruction in laboratory models of arthritis. Epidemiological studies suggest regular green tea consumption is associated with lower rates of arthritis and reduced inflammatory markers.

How to Use

  • Drink 2–3 cups of green tea daily — brew at 70–80°C (not boiling) for 2–3 minutes
  • Matcha provides concentrated EGCG
  • Green tea supplements are available but may interact with some medications

Black Pepper (Piper nigrum)

The Evidence

Piperine, the active compound in black pepper, has anti-inflammatory properties and — crucially — dramatically improves the absorption of curcumin from turmeric (by up to 2,000%). It also enhances the bioavailability of other beneficial compounds. Always combine turmeric with black pepper for maximum benefit.

Combining Herbs and Spices

A practical approach to incorporating anti-inflammatory herbs and spices into your daily routine:

  • Morning — Golden milk (warm milk with ½ tsp turmeric, pinch of black pepper, ½ tsp cinnamon, ½ tsp ginger)
  • Lunch — Add fresh garlic and rosemary to soups or salads
  • Afternoon — Green tea
  • Dinner — Cook with ginger, garlic and plenty of herbs and spices

While individual spices may have modest effects, the cumulative benefit of an overall anti-inflammatory dietary pattern — rich in herbs, spices, fruits, vegetables and whole grains — is well supported by evidence. Our virtual assistant can help you plan anti-inflammatory meals using these ingredients.

This article is for general information only. Herbs and spices complement but do not replace medical treatment. Consult your GP before taking herbal supplements, particularly if you take prescription medications.

### Practical next steps for Anti-Inflammatory Herbs and Spices for Arthritis: A Complete Guide If you came here about **Anti-Inflammatory Herbs and Spices for Arthritis: A Complete Guide**, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete. In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live. ### Everyday eating patterns No single food cures arthritis. Patterns rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses, wholegrains and oily fish are the ones most often discussed in UK dietetic advice for inflammatory conditions. Keep changes realistic: swap one ultra-processed snack for fruit and nuts, or cook with olive oil more often than seed oils marketed as miracle cures. ### Everyday eating patterns No single food cures arthritis. Patterns rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses, wholegrains and oily fish are the ones most often discussed in UK dietetic advice for inflammatory conditions. Keep changes realistic: swap one ultra-processed snack for fruit and nuts, or cook with olive oil more often than seed oils marketed as miracle cures. ### Quick questions about Anti Inflammatory Herbs Spices **Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician?** No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team. **How long before I judge whether a change helped?** Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner. **What should I track?** Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings. ### Safety and when to get urgent help This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous. ### Keep learning with us Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis UK — try the [guides hub](/guides), [diet hub](/diet), [exercise hub](/exercises), or [site search](/search) to filter by topic and length. article.title: Arthritis in Young Adults: Recognising It Early
article.excerpt: Arthritis is not just an older person’s condition. Reactive arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and more commonly begin in your 20s and 30s — and diagnosis is often delayed because of it.
article.content:
Quick answer: Several forms of arthritis, including reactive arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis, characteristically begin in a person’s 20s or 30s. Diagnosis is often delayed because joint pain in younger adults is frequently attributed to injury or posture rather than investigated for inflammatory disease — persistence in seeking assessment matters, since untreated inflammation causes more damage the longer it continues.

## Arthritis Isn't Just an "Older Person's" Condition Arthritis carries a stubborn stereotype as something that only affects older people, which means younger adults with real joint symptoms are sometimes dismissed — by friends, family, and occasionally by health services — before they're taken seriously. In reality, several forms of arthritis specifically affect younger people, and getting an early, accurate diagnosis matters just as much at 25 as it does at 65, arguably more, since untreated inflammatory arthritis has more years ahead of it to cause joint damage. ## Types of Arthritis More Common in Younger Adults - **Reactive arthritis** typically develops in people in their 20s and 30s, triggered by an infection elsewhere in the body (commonly a gut or genital infection) days to weeks earlier. It often resolves within months but can become longer-lasting in some people. - **Ankylosing spondylitis** usually first causes symptoms — typically lower back pain and stiffness — in the late teens to early 30s, and is frequently misattributed to posture, gym injuries, or general back strain for years before diagnosis. - **Juvenile idiopathic arthritis**, diagnosed in childhood, can persist into adulthood, meaning many "young adults" with arthritis have actually been managing it since childhood. - **Psoriatic arthritis** can develop at any age but often appears in people already living with psoriasis in their 20s to 40s. - **Rheumatoid arthritis**, while more common later in life, does affect younger adults too, and early-onset cases are sometimes more aggressive if not caught quickly. ## Why Diagnosis Is Often Delayed Younger adults with joint pain face a specific set of obstacles to getting diagnosed quickly: - **Assumption bias** — both patients and clinicians can unconsciously assume joint pain in a young person is more likely to be an injury, overuse, or unrelated to arthritis, delaying the right tests. - **Symptoms attributed to lifestyle** — back pain in a 25-year-old is more likely to be blamed on posture, gym training, or a mattress than investigated for inflammatory disease, even when the pattern (worse at night, improves with movement, morning stiffness over 30 minutes) points toward something like ankylosing spondylitis. - **Normal or borderline blood tests** — some younger patients with genuine inflammatory arthritis have blood markers within a "normal" range, which can be misread as ruling out arthritis entirely rather than prompting further specialist assessment. - **Reluctance to push for referral** — many younger adults, especially early in their working lives, are hesitant to repeatedly go back to their GP about ongoing symptoms, which can add months of delay. The practical takeaway: if joint pain or stiffness — particularly back stiffness that's worse first thing in the morning and eases with movement, or joint swelling that doesn't resolve — persists for more than a few weeks, it's worth asking directly about a rheumatology referral rather than waiting to see if it resolves on its own. ## The Cost of Delayed Diagnosis For inflammatory types of arthritis in particular, the gap between symptom onset and diagnosis matters. Ankylosing spondylitis, for example, has historically taken years to diagnose from first symptoms in many cases, partly because it was under-recognised in younger patients. During that delay, ongoing inflammation can cause changes to the spine that are harder to reverse than if treatment had started early. This is one of the strongest arguments for younger adults being persistent about unexplained, persistent joint symptoms rather than accepting reassurance that "you're too young for arthritis." ## Managing Arthritis Alongside Work, Study and Family Life A diagnosis in your 20s or 30s comes with a different set of practical challenges than one later in life — often balancing a chronic condition against building a career, studying, starting a family, or simply the busy pace of that life stage. - **Workplace adjustments** — in the UK, arthritis can qualify as a disability under the Equality Act 2010, meaning employers have a legal duty to consider reasonable adjustments (flexible hours, ergonomic equipment, modified duties during flares). - **Fertility and pregnancy planning** — some arthritis medications need to be reviewed or changed before trying to conceive; this is worth raising proactively with a rheumatologist rather than waiting until pregnancy is already underway. - **Energy management** — fatigue from inflammatory arthritis can be as limiting as joint pain itself; pacing activity across the week, rather than pushing hard on good days and crashing afterward, tends to work better long-term. - **Mental health** — receiving a lifelong diagnosis at a younger age can bring a real sense of loss or anxiety about the future; connecting with others managing the same condition, whether through a support group or online community, consistently helps people process this. ## Staying Active With a Younger-Onset Diagnosis Contrary to a common fear, most people with inflammatory or joint conditions are encouraged to stay active rather than avoid exercise. The right type of activity depends on the specific condition and which joints are affected, but in general: - Low-impact cardio (swimming, cycling) protects joints while maintaining fitness - Core and back-strengthening exercise is specifically recommended for ankylosing spondylitis to help maintain posture and spinal mobility - Sport and exercise can usually continue with modifications during a flare rather than being abandoned altogether - A physiotherapist experienced in inflammatory arthritis can build a plan around your specific goals, whether that's returning to a sport or simply staying comfortable day to day ## Building a Long-Term Relationship With a Rheumatology Team Being diagnosed young often means decades of an ongoing relationship with rheumatology services, which is worth approaching differently than a short-term treatment plan. It's worth being an active participant in appointments — keeping notes on symptom patterns between visits, being honest about medication side effects rather than quietly stopping treatment, and asking directly about the long-term goals of your treatment plan (many services now aim for full remission as a realistic target, not just symptom control). Transition from paediatric to adult rheumatology services, for those diagnosed with juvenile arthritis, is a particular point worth planning for actively, since continuity of care can otherwise be lost during the handover. ## Sport, Relationships and Social Life A younger-onset diagnosis doesn't have to mean giving up an active social or sporting life, though it may mean adapting how you approach it. Being open with teammates, training partners or close friends about flare-ups — rather than pushing through silently — tends to lead to more sustainable participation over time than either overexerting or withdrawing entirely. Dating and relationships can raise their own questions about when and how to talk about a chronic condition; there's no single right answer, but many people find that treating it as a normal part of who they are, rather than something to hide, leads to more supportive relationships in the long run. ## Frequently Asked Questions **Can you get arthritis in your 20s?** Yes. Reactive arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis and even rheumatoid arthritis can all begin in your 20s, and juvenile arthritis diagnosed in childhood often continues into adulthood. **Why did it take so long to get diagnosed?** Delayed diagnosis in younger adults is a well-recognised pattern, often due to symptoms being attributed to injury, posture or overuse rather than investigated for inflammatory arthritis. If you're facing ongoing delay, asking directly for a rheumatology referral can help. **Will arthritis affect my ability to have children?** Most people with arthritis can have healthy pregnancies, though some medications need reviewing beforehand. This is best planned proactively with your rheumatology team rather than left until later. **Is reactive arthritis permanent?** Often not — many cases resolve within several months of the triggering infection clearing. Some people do go on to have longer-lasting symptoms, which is why follow-up with a rheumatologist is worthwhile even after the initial flare settles. ## Key Takeaways - Several forms of arthritis, including reactive arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis, characteristically begin in younger adulthood. - Diagnosis is often delayed in younger patients due to assumptions that joint pain "can't be arthritis" at a young age. - Delayed treatment of inflammatory arthritis allows more time for joint or spinal damage to occur — persistence in seeking a diagnosis matters. - UK employment law provides real protections and adjustment rights for younger adults managing a chronic joint condition at work. - Staying active, with the right guidance, remains encouraged rather than restricted for most younger adults with arthritis. *This article provides general information and is not a substitute for personalised medical advice. If you have persistent joint pain or stiffness, speak to your GP about further assessment regardless of your age.*

article.title: Best Knee Exercises for Arthritis
article.excerpt: Physiotherapist-approved knee exercises to strengthen muscles, reduce pain and improve mobility with arthritis.
article.content:
Quick answer: Knee exercises are beneficial for arthritis by strengthening muscles, particularly the quadriceps, which can act as shock absorbers and reduce cartilage load. Key exercises include straight leg raises, wall sits, step-ups, hamstring curls, calf raises, and seated knee extensions, performed consistently three times a week. These help reduce pain and improve physical function.

## Why Knee Exercises Matter The knee is the joint most commonly affected by osteoarthritis in the UK. Strong muscles around the knee — particularly the quadriceps — act as shock absorbers, reducing the load on damaged cartilage by up to 30%. ### The Evidence Exercise is one of the most consistently supported treatments for knee osteoarthritis in the medical literature. A 2023 individual-participant-data meta-analysis in *The Lancet Rheumatology*, combining results across multiple randomised trials of knee and hip osteoarthritis, found that therapeutic exercise produces a real, if modest, improvement in pain and physical function compared with not exercising — a finding echoed by NICE guidance, which recommends exercise as a core treatment for knee OA regardless of age, pain severity or disability. The effect size varies between studies and individuals, and exercise alone will not eliminate symptoms for everyone — but consistently doing the right exercises remains one of the few interventions with a genuine, evidence-based track record for this condition. ### The 6 Best Knee Exercises #### 1. Straight Leg Raises Lie on your back, one knee bent. Tighten your thigh muscle and slowly raise your straight leg to the height of the bent knee. Hold 5 seconds. Lower slowly. - **Sets/Reps:** 3 × 10 each leg - **Why it works:** Strengthens quadriceps without bending the knee #### 2. Wall Sits Stand with your back against a wall. Slide down until your knees are at about 45 degrees (not 90°). Hold for 10–30 seconds. - **Sets:** 3 × 15–30 seconds - **Why it works:** Builds isometric quad strength #### 3. Step-Ups Using a low step (10–15 cm), step up leading with your affected leg. Step down slowly. - **Sets/Reps:** 2 × 10 each leg - **Why it works:** Functional strengthening for stairs #### 4. Hamstring Curls Stand holding a chair. Slowly bend one knee, bringing your heel toward your buttock. Hold 3 seconds. - **Sets/Reps:** 3 × 10 each leg - **Why it works:** Balances muscle support around the knee #### 5. Calf Raises Stand on both feet, slowly rise onto your toes. Hold 3 seconds. Lower slowly. - **Sets/Reps:** 3 × 12 - **Why it works:** Supports ankle stability and reduces knee strain #### 6. Seated Knee Extensions Sit in a chair. Slowly straighten one leg, hold 5 seconds, then lower. - **Sets/Reps:** 3 × 10 each leg - **Why it works:** Gentle quad strengthening for flare-up days ### Golden Rules 1. **Start gently** — begin with fewer reps and build up 2. **Dull ache is OK**, sharp pain is not — stop if you feel sharp pain 3. **Apply the 24-hour rule** — if your knee is worse 24 hours later, you did too much 4. **Consistency beats intensity** — 3× weekly for 8 weeks minimum 5. **Warm up first** — 5 minutes of gentle walking *Programme by James Walker, MCSP, HCPC Registered Physiotherapist* ### Practical next steps for Best Knee Exercises for Arthritis If you came here about **Best Knee Exercises for Arthritis**, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete. In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live. ### Building a joint-friendly routine Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery. ### Pacing on good and bad days On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether. ### Working with NHS pathways Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates. ### Quick questions about Best Knee Exercises Arthritis **Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician?** No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team. **How long before I judge whether a change helped?** Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner. **What should I track?** Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings. ### Safety and when to get urgent help This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous. ### Keep learning with us Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis UK — try the [guides hub](/guides), [diet hub](/diet), [exercise hub](/exercises), or [site search](/search) to filter by topic and length. article.title: Berries and Antioxidants: Food Medicine for Inflammation
article.excerpt: Anthocyanins in berries down-regulate inflammatory pathways linked to arthritis pain. UK-available berries, portion sizes and easy daily uses.
article.content:
Quick answer: Evidence in this guide frames arthritis pain as multifactorial, with inflammatory and degenerative patterns needing different management. It highlights structured movement, Mediterranean-style anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, heat or cold, and sleep habits as helpful. Start small, track simple weekly outcomes, and seek GP or physiotherapy advice for red, swollen joints, weight loss, prolonged morning stiffness, numbness or weakness.

## What this guide covers This piece summarises what the current evidence says about **berries and antioxidants: food medicine for inflammation**, the practical steps that help most, and the red flags that mean you should speak to your GP or physiotherapist. It is written for people living in the UK and reviewed by our clinical team. ## The underlying mechanism Arthritis pain rarely has a single cause. Joint cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, surrounding muscle and the nervous system all contribute. Understanding which of these is driving your specific symptom is the first step toward targeted relief. For an in-depth condition overview, see our [related guide](/diet). Inflammatory and degenerative forms behave differently. Inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid, psoriatic, ankylosing spondylitis) typically worsens with rest and improves with gentle movement. Degenerative arthritis (osteoarthritis) typically worsens with prolonged use. Knowing which pattern matches your day-to-day experience helps you choose the right management approach. ## What helps — by strength of evidence 1. **Movement and graded exercise.** NICE NG226 (2022) and Cochrane reviews place structured exercise as a first-line treatment. article.title: Joint Fusion vs Replacement: How Surgeons Choose
article.excerpt: The case for fusion in ankles, wrists and small joints.
article.content:
Quick answer: Joint replacement is often preferred for large, weight-bearing joints like the hip and knee, aiming for improved function. Conversely, joint fusion is frequently considered for smaller joints such as those in the wrist or foot, and particularly the ankle, offering pain relief and stability. Both surgeries are typically considered when non-surgical treatments are no longer effective and quality of life is severely impacted.

## Overview The case for fusion in ankles, wrists and small joints. ## What the evidence shows UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Versus Arthritis consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus. ## What this means for you - **Talk to your clinician.** Personalised advice always beats blanket rules. - **Track your symptoms.** Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days. - **Move within comfort.** Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood. - **Watch the warning signs.** New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review. ## Practical next steps 1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: [related guidance](/exercises/ankle). 2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment. 3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day. ## Editorial standards This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis Editorial Team and reviewed by our Clinical Review Board against UK NICE guidance and peer-reviewed sources. We update content at least annually. ## What the Evidence Says Current research consistently highlights the importance of a step-wise approach to managing arthritis, starting with non-surgical options. Randomised trials and systematic reviews show that a combination of exercise, physical therapy, and appropriate medications can significantly improve joint function and reduce pain for many people. Surgical interventions, such as joint fusion or replacement, are typically considered when these conservative treatments are no longer effective and a person's quality of life is severely impacted. Clinical guidelines from leading medical bodies across the UK emphasise shared decision-making, where the person with arthritis and their healthcare team discuss all available options, weighing up the potential benefits and risks of each. The focus is on preserving natural joint function where possible and, when surgery is necessary, choosing the procedure most likely to offer long-term relief and improved mobility, tailored to the individual's specific circumstances and the affected joint. For smaller joints, like those in the wrist or foot, and particularly for the ankle, fusion (arthrodesis) is often considered a reliable option for pain relief and stability, especially in specific arthritis types. Conversely, for larger, weight-bearing joints like the hip and knee, joint replacement (arthroplasty) often provides superior functional outcomes. The evidence for these preferences is built on decades of patient outcomes and ongoing surgical technique refinements. ## Common Mistakes to Avoid * **Ignoring early symptoms:** Hoping pain will simply go away on its own. *Fix: Keep a symptom diary and discuss persistent pain with your family doctor.* * **Overdoing it on good days:** Pushing through significant pain, leading to flare-ups. *Fix: Pace yourself and listen to your body, even when feeling well.* * **Stopping medication without advice:** Discontinuing prescribed drugs because you feel better. *Fix: Always consult your doctor before making changes to your medication.* * **Avoiding all movement:** Fearing that exercise will damage your joints further. *Fix: Engage in gentle, recommended exercises to maintain strength and flexibility.* * **Self-diagnosing online and delaying professional help:** Relying solely on internet searches for treatment plans. *Fix: Seek professional medical advice for an accurate diagnosis and personalised care plan.* ## When to Speak to a Clinician It's important to reach out to your GP, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist if you notice significant changes in your joint health. Don't wait for your next routine appointment if you experience any of the following: * Sudden, severe increase in joint pain. * New or rapidly worsening joint swelling or redness. * Feeling generally unwell with a fever alongside joint pain. * Rapid loss of movement or function in a joint. * Joint pain that keeps you awake at night or is present at rest. ## Frequently Asked Questions ### What happens if I delay treatment for arthritis? Delaying effective treatment can lead to worsening joint damage and increased pain over time. Early intervention, including medication and lifestyle adjustments, can help slow the progression of the disease and preserve joint function. ### How long does recovery take after joint surgery? Recovery time varies greatly depending on the type of surgery, the joint involved, and your overall health. For some, it might be a few weeks, while for more complex procedures, it could be several months of rehabilitation. Your surgical team will provide a tailored recovery plan. ### Can I still be active after joint fusion or replacement? Absolutely. The goal of these surgeries is often to reduce pain and improve your ability to move. While some activities might need to be modified, many people return to a good level of activity, including walking, swimming, and cycling, following successful recovery. ### Practical next steps for Joint Fusion vs Replacement: How Surgeons Choose If you came here about **Joint Fusion vs Replacement: How Surgeons Choose**, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. article.title: Joint Replacement Surgery for Arthritis — A Complete UK Guide
article.excerpt: Everything you need to know about knee and hip replacement surgery on the NHS: when it's right, what to expect, and how to prepare and recover.
article.content:
Clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Last updated: June 2026.

Quick answer: Joint replacement surgery is considered when severe, persistent pain affects daily activities and sleep, other treatments have failed, X-rays show significant joint damage, and quality of life is impacted. In the UK, over 200,000 hip and knee replacements occur annually, and more than 90% of people report significant improvement in pain and mobility.

Joint replacement surgery sounds daunting. It is natural to feel anxious — but it is also one of the most successful operations in modern medicine. In the UK, more than 200,000 hip and knee replacements are performed each year, and over 90% of people report significant improvement in pain and mobility.

This guide explains everything in plain English, from deciding if surgery is right for you to what recovery actually feels like.

When Is Joint Replacement the Right Choice?

Joint replacement is not the first option. You and your doctor will usually consider it when you have severe persistent pain affecting your sleep and daily activities, other treatments have not provided enough relief, X-rays show significant joint damage, and your quality of life is being seriously affected. It is a decision you make with your orthopaedic surgeon, not one they make for you.

Knee Replacement Surgery — What to Expect

A total knee replacement (knee arthroplasty) involves removing the damaged surfaces of the knee joint and replacing them with metal and plastic implants. The operation takes about 1–2 hours, usually under spinal anaesthetic or general anaesthetic. You will typically stay in hospital for 1–3 days. You will be encouraged to stand and take a few steps with a walking frame within 24 hours, and a physiotherapist will guide you through the first exercises. Most people notice improved mobility within 6–12 weeks, with continued gains for up to a year.

Hip Replacement Surgery — Recovery and Results

Hip replacements follow a similar pattern to knee replacements. The damaged ball-and-socket joint is replaced with artificial components. Hip replacement generally has a slightly quicker early recovery than knee replacement. Many people go home within 1–2 days. Use crutches or a walking frame for 2–6 weeks, follow hip precautions if advised, and most people can drive after about 6 weeks (check with your insurance provider). You may return to work within 6–12 weeks depending on your job.

Getting on the NHS Waiting List

The pathway typically involves GP referral to an orthopaedic consultant, specialist assessment with X-ray review, decision to proceed, pre-operative assessment (blood tests, heart tracing, health checks), and finally a surgery date. The NHS Constitution target is a maximum of 18 weeks from referral to treatment, but waits may be longer in some areas.

Preparing for Surgery (Pre-habilitation)

What you do before surgery significantly affects how well you recover after. Strengthen your muscles around the joint — stronger muscles mean faster recovery. Maintain a healthy weight — excess weight puts extra stress on your new joint and increases surgical risks. Stop smoking — it slows healing and raises complication risks. Eat well, and plan your home: arrange help with shopping, cooking, and transport for the first few weeks, and clear trip hazards.

Recovery Timeline and Rehabilitation

Everyone recovers at their own pace. Week 1–2: walking with a frame or crutches inside the house, daily physio exercises, swelling and discomfort peak then improve. Weeks 2–6: gradually reduce walking aids, start walking outside, continue exercises. Weeks 6–12: walking freely, return to driving, may return to office-based work. 3–6 months: significant improvement in pain and function. 6–12 months: continued gains, resume low-impact sports. Knee replacements tend to have a slightly slower recovery than hips.

Life After Joint Replacement

The goal is a life with less pain and more movement. Most people can walk without pain, sleep through the night, return to hobbies like gardening and swimming, and travel comfortably. You should avoid high-impact activities like running or jumping. Modern implants often last 15–25 years or more.

Alternatives to Surgery

Surgery is not the only way forward. Some people manage well with weight loss (even 5–10% of body weight can significantly reduce knee pain), a tailored physiotherapy exercise programme, a pain management programme combining physical and psychological strategies, walking aids and supports, or steroid injections for temporary relief. Always explore these with your GP or physiotherapist first.
